title: STAT 579: Final Project Hub
text:
Welcome to the central hub for the STAT 579 final project. This page contains everything you need to successfully complete your target trial emulation, from initial guidelines to final grading rubrics. Please bookmark this page and refer to it often throughout the semester.
The goal of this project is to give you hands-on experience in conducting a causal inference study from start to finish. You will pose a causal question, design a hypothetical “target trial” to answer it, and then use real-world observational data to emulate that trial. This process will challenge you to be rigorous, thoughtful, and transparent about your assumptions.

title: Worksheet 1: Uncovering Confounding with Simpson’s Paradox
text: Hello class. This worksheet is designed to give you hands-on practice with the concepts we discussed in Lecture 1. The goal is not just to get the right answer, but to understand the process of thinking causally.

title: Worksheet 1: Uncovering Confounding with Simpson’s Paradox
text:
Background / Scenario
A hospital has conducted a study comparing two treatments for kidney stones:

Treatment A: A new, advanced surgical procedure.
Treatment B: The standard, less invasive treatment.

The hospital has provided you with data on 400 patients who received one of the two treatments. The outcome of interest is whether the treatment was a success (i.e., the kidney stones were completely removed).
Here is the raw data:

title: Worksheet 1: Uncovering Confounding with Simpson’s Paradox
text:
Learning Objective
By the end of this worksheet, you will be able to:

Calculate and compare crude (overall) rates of success.
Identify a potential confounding variable from a problem description.
Perform a stratified analysis to calculate group-specific rates.
Explain how confounding can lead to Simpson’s Paradox, where group-specific trends are reversed in the aggregate data.
Draw a simple Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG) to represent the relationships between variables.

title: Worksheet 1: Uncovering Confounding with Simpson’s Paradox
text:
Step-by-Step Scaffolding Tasks

Step 1: The Naive (Overall) Comparison
First, let’s look at the data from a purely associational perspective, ignoring any other factors.

Task 1a: Calculate the overall success rate for patients who received Treatment A.

Guiding Question: What is the total number of patients who had a success with Treatment A? What is the total number of patients who received Treatment A?
Calculation: (Number of Successes for A) / (Total Number receiving A) = ?

Task 1b: Calculate the overall success rate for patients who received Treatment B.

Calculation: (Number of Successes for B) / (Total Number receiving B) = ?

Task 1c: Based only on these overall rates, which treatment appears to be more effective?




Step 2: Identifying a Potential Confounder
In our lecture, we discussed that observational comparisons can be misleading. A key piece of information was left out of the table above: doctors tend to assign the more invasive Treatment A to patients with large kidney stones, while patients with small stones often receive the standard Treatment B. Stone size is also known to affect the difficulty of the treatment.

Task 2a: In this scenario, what is the third variable that might be related to both the treatment assigned and the treatment’s success? This is our potential confounder.
Task 2b: Explain why this variable could be a confounder.

Guiding Question: How might stone size influence a doctor’s choice of treatment? How might stone size independently influence whether a treatment is successful?





Step 3: The Stratified Analysis (Controlling for the Confounder)
Now, let’s re-examine the data, but this time we will “stratify” it by stone size. This is like looking at the data for small stones and large stones separately.
Here is the complete data, broken down by stone size:

Task 3a: Calculate the success rate for each treatment only for patients with small stones.

Success Rate for A (Small Stones): ? / ? = ?
Success Rate for B (Small Stones): ? / ? = ?
Which treatment is better for this group?

Task 3b: Calculate the success rate for each treatment only for patients with large stones.

Success Rate for A (Large Stones): ? / ? = ?
Success Rate for B (Large Stones): ? / ? = ?
Which treatment is better for this group?




Step 4: Visualizing the Causal Structure (DAG)
Let’s draw a map of our causal assumptions.

Task 4: Create a Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG) with three nodes: Treatment Choice, Stone Size, and Success. Draw arrows to represent the causal relationships you uncovered in the steps above.

Guiding Questions:

Does the treatment choice cause a successful outcome? (This is the arrow we hope to understand). Draw it.
Does the patient’s stone size cause the doctor to choose a particular treatment? Draw it.
Does the stone size cause a treatment to be more or less successful, regardless of which treatment is used? Draw it.

title: Worksheet 1: Uncovering Confounding with Simpson’s Paradox
text:
Reflection / Discussion Questions

Compare your answer from Task 1c with your answers from Task 3a and Task 3b. What do you notice? This reversal is known as Simpson’s Paradox.
Explain, in your own words, why Treatment A looked worse in the overall analysis but better in both the small-stone and large-stone groups. (Hint: Think about which group of patients was disproportionately receiving Treatment A).
What does this exercise teach you about the danger of drawing causal conclusions from simple, overall comparisons of two groups in observational data?

title: Worksheet 1: Uncovering Confounding with Simpson’s Paradox
text:
Optional Challenge
Imagine a different variable: Post-operative Care Unit. Suppose all patients who get Treatment A are sent to ICU Care, while patients getting Treatment B are sent to Standard Care. A researcher decides to “control” for this by stratifying the analysis by care unit. Why might this be a mistake? Think about the timing. Can the choice of care unit be a common cause of both treatment and success, or is it something else? (This touches on the concept of a mediator, which we will discuss later in the course).

title: How to Write a Great Critique
text:
Welcome to the central guide for your weekly paper critiques. The goal of this assignment is to train you not just to understand a paper, but to deconstruct its argument, question its assumptions, and situate it within the broader field of causal inference.
Our course uses a unique mix of readings: foundational methodological papers, applied case studies, and modern textbook chapters. Your critique assignment asks you to focus on the foundational paper for each week, but the key to an excellent critique is to skillfully synthesize insights from all three sources.


Depending on the paper, you will need to wear one of two hats: the theoretician’s hat for methodological papers or the peer reviewer’s hat for case studies.


(Applies to papers like Rubin 1974, Pearl 1995, Rosenbaum & Rubin 1983)
When a paper proposes a method, your critique should focus on the validity, logic, and impact of that method. Since there is no data analysis, you must analyze the abstract argument.
Use this four-step process to structure your thinking:

Deconstruct the Problem & Proposed Solution:

The Problem: What specific challenge in causal inference is the paper trying to solve? (e.g., How can we control for many confounders at once? How do we define a causal effect?)
The Solution: What is the paper’s core contribution? Explain the new concept (e.g., potential outcomes, propensity scores, DAGs) in your own words.

Analyze the Logic & Identification Strategy:

The “Why”: What is the central logical argument for why their solution works? Explain the intuition behind any theorems or proofs. (e.g., The authors prove the propensity score is a balancing score, meaning…)
The Assumptions: What are the precise assumptions needed for this logic to hold? (e.g., This entire framework rests on the untestable assumption of strong ignorability…)

Scrutinize the Assumptions & Plausibility:

Real-World Plausibility: In what kinds of real-world studies would these assumptions be plausible? Where would they likely fail? Use examples from the case study or your own knowledge.
Failure Modes: What are the practical limitations of the method? (e.g., The method offers no protection against unmeasured confounding and is sensitive to violations of the positivity assumption.)

Evaluate the Impact & Legacy:

The Impact: How did this paper change the field? What did it make possible?
The Legacy: What subsequent research or methods did it inspire? What is its biggest remaining limitation?





(Applies to papers like Yusuf et al. 1991, Snowden et al. 2011, and all of the “Expedition” readings)
When a paper makes a causal claim about the world using data, your critique should focus on the credibility of that claim. Your job is to act as a rigorous, skeptical peer reviewer.

Scrutinize the Causal Question & Design:

The Question: Is the causal question well-defined (PICO)? Is the target trial clear?
The Data: Is the data source appropriate? Are there risks of major measurement error?

Interrogate the Identification Strategy:

The DAG: Draw a DAG for this specific study, reflecting its variables and context.
Attack the Key Assumption: This is the core of your critique. Is the central assumption (e.g., unconfoundedness, parallel trends, exclusion restriction) plausible in this specific context? What unmeasured confounder or alternative explanation did the authors likely miss?

Audit the Diagnostics & Analysis:

The Diagnostics: Did the authors perform and show the essential diagnostic checks for their method? (e.g., balance plots for propensity scores; first-stage F-statistic for IV).
The Model: Was the statistical model appropriate for the outcome and data structure?

Challenge the Interpretation & Conclusion:

The Interpretation: Do the authors overstate their claims? Do they acknowledge their key limitations?
The Sensitivity Analysis: Did they quantify how robust their finding is to unmeasured confounding (e.g., with an E-value)? If not, it is a major weakness.
The Generalizability: Do they correctly interpret the scope of their finding (e.g., acknowledging a LATE is not an ATE)?






Your assignment is to critique the foundational paper. You will use the other readings to become a smarter critic.
Your Task: Critique Rosenbaum & Rubin (1983), “The central role of the propensity score…”

Start with the Map (Textbook): You read Hernán & Robins, Chapter 12. You now have a modern understanding of propensity scores, the ATE, and balancing diagnostics.
Critique the Journal (Foundational Paper): You apply the “How to Critique a Foundational Paper” framework to Rosenbaum & Rubin (1983).

Problem: The paper addresses the problem of controlling for many confounders in observational studies.
Solution: It introduces the propensity score as a single-number summary for balancing covariates.
Logic: It proves the balancing property of the score.
Assumption: The entire method relies on the assumption of strong ignorability (unconfoundedness).

Enrich with the Expedition (Case Study): Now, you use Dehejia & Wahba (1999) to add depth to your critique.

In your section on Assumption Plausibility, you write: “Rosenbaum & Rubin’s framework is entirely dependent on the unconfoundedness assumption. The Dehejia & Wahba (1999) case study provides an ideal scenario where this assumption is arguably plausible. By using a rich administrative dataset with detailed pre-treatment earnings and employment histories, they were able to control for the most likely determinants of both entering the training program and future earnings.”
In your section on Impact & Legacy, you write: “A key limitation of the original paper is its focus on theory, with little guidance on diagnostics. The profound impact of this work is demonstrated in applications like Dehejia & Wahba, which established the now-standard practice of reporting standardized mean differences in a balance plot to empirically verify that the propensity score did, in fact, balance the observed covariates.”


By following this process, you are not critiquing the case study; you are using it as evidence to make your critique of the foundational paper more concrete, critical, and insightful.

text:

section: STAT 579: Rubric for Weekly Paper Critiques
text:
STAT 579: Rubric for Weekly Paper Critiques
This rubric outlines the criteria for evaluating your weekly paper critiques posted on the Canvas Discussion forum. The goal is to reward thoughtful engagement with the material, clear reasoning, and a critical, assumption-focused perspective.

1. Rubric for Student Critiques (Participants)
This rubric is for all students who are not the designated Discussion Leader for the week. Each critique is worth a total of 20 points.










Dimension
Excellent (A-Level Work)
Good (B-Level Work)
Needs Improvement (C-Level or Below)
Points




Answers to Guiding Questions
Answers are not just correct but demonstrate deep, critical engagement with the paper. The student uses examples, connects concepts to the broader course, and writes with analytical depth.
Answers are generally correct and address all parts of the prompt. The analysis is sound but may be more descriptive than critical.
Answers are incomplete, factually incorrect, or demonstrate a superficial understanding of the core concepts.
/ 12


Clarity & Reasoning
The writing is clear, logical, and easy to follow. The student effectively communicates complex statistical ideas in their own words.
The writing is mostly clear, but may contain some jargon or slightly convoluted phrasing. The core logic is sound.
The writing is unclear, making the argument difficult to follow. Key terms may be used incorrectly.
/ 4


Takeaway & Critical Perspective
The takeaway is insightful, goes beyond a simple summary, and shows critical reflection on the paper’s assumptions, limitations, or broader implications.
The takeaway is reasonable and relevant to the paper, but may not offer a deep or novel insight.
The takeaway is a simple restatement of a fact from the paper, is unrelated to the core argument, or is missing.
/ 4





2. Rubric for the Weekly Discussion Leader
The weekly Discussion Leader is evaluated on the same 20-point scale but with criteria re-weighted to reflect their role in framing the conversation for the class.










Dimension
Excellent (A-Level Work)
Good (B-Level Work)
Needs Improvement (C-Level or Below)
Points




Summary & Synthesis
The summary is comprehensive, accurate, and skillfully frames the paper’s context, core argument, and importance. It provides a strong foundation for the class discussion.
The summary is accurate and covers the main points but may lack depth in explaining the paper’s broader significance or context.
The summary contains significant inaccuracies, is incomplete, or fails to identify the paper’s central contribution.
/ 8


Answers to Guiding Questions
Answers are exemplary, serving as a model of deep analysis for the class. They are well-reasoned and demonstrate a superior grasp of the material.
Answers are correct and thoughtful, addressing all parts of the prompt.
Answers are superficial, incorrect, or suggest a misunderstanding of the guiding questions.
/ 6


Posing New Questions
The two self-generated questions are insightful, open-ended, and designed to stimulate high-level discussion and critical thinking beyond the provided questions.
The questions are relevant but may be more straightforward or less provocative (e.g., closer to comprehension checks).
The questions are simple comprehension checks, are unclear, unrelated to the core themes, or are missing.
/ 6

title: STAT 579: Project Proposal Grading Rubric
text:
This rubric outlines the criteria for evaluating your project proposal. The proposal is graded out of 50 points and accounts for 10% of your final course grade. The goal of this deliverable is to ensure that you have a well-defined, feasible, and causally-grounded research plan.










Component
Weight
Criteria for Excellence (A)
Criteria for Proficiency (B)
Criteria for Developing (C/Below)




Causal Question & Motivation
10 pts
The causal question is specific, clear, and unambiguous. The motivation is compelling, grounded in public health/scientific relevance, and supported by appropriate citations.
The question is causal but could be more specific. The motivation is present but may be overly broad or not well-supported.
The question is associational, vague, or poorly defined. The motivation is unclear or absent.


Data Source
10 pts
The proposed dataset is clearly identified and is appropriate for the causal question. Key variables (exposure, outcome, confounders) are correctly identified.
A dataset is identified, but its appropriateness is not fully justified. The list of key variables may be incomplete.
No specific dataset is identified, or the chosen dataset is clearly unsuitable for the research question.


Causal Model (DAG)
15 pts
The DAG is plausible, clearly drawn, and includes the key exposure, outcome, and confounders. The justification for the DAG’s structure is thoughtful and demonstrates a strong understanding of the topic.
The DAG is present but may be overly simplistic or contain questionable causal arrows. The justification is superficial.
The DAG is missing, illegible, or fundamentally incorrect (e.g., contains cycles, reverses obvious causal pathways).


Target Trial Protocol
10 pts
The key components of the target trial (eligibility, treatment strategies, outcome) are clearly and precisely defined, demonstrating a strong grasp of the emulation framework.
The target trial components are listed but may be vague or poorly aligned with the causal question and data.
The target trial protocol is not described or is fundamentally misunderstood.


Proposed Method(s) & Feasibility
5 pts
The proposed causal method is appropriate for the question and data. The plan is feasible within the scope of the course, and potential challenges are acknowledged.
A causal method is proposed but may not be the most appropriate. The feasibility of the plan is questionable.
No causal method is proposed, or the proposed method is incorrect for the stated problem.

title: STAT 579: Final Project Proposal
text:
This document serves as the proposal for the STAT 579 final project. The goal is to provide a clear, concise, and feasible plan for your target trial emulation. Please replace the instructional text (in italics) with your own content. The final proposal should be approximately 2-3 pages.

1. The Causal Question

State your primary research question in a single, clear sentence. It must be a causal question (e.g., “What is the causal effect of X on Y?”) and not merely associational.



2. Scientific Background and Motivation

In 1-2 paragraphs, explain the public health or scientific relevance of your question. Why is this an important question to answer? What is already known on the topic? Briefly cite 2-3 key references that motivate your study.



3. Data Source

Identify the observational dataset you will use. Describe the source of the data (e.g., NHANES 2017-2018 cycle, MIMIC-IV v2.0). List the key variables you plan to use for your exposure (A), outcome (Y), and the primary confounders (L) you identified in your DAG.



4. Preliminary Causal Model (DAG)

Insert an image of your Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG) here. The DAG should represent your current understanding of the causal relationships between the exposure, outcome, and key covariates. Below the image, provide a brief (1 paragraph) justification for the structure, explaining the most important causal pathways and confounding variables.



5. Target Trial Emulation Protocol

Briefly outline the key components of your target trial protocol. You can do this in a bulleted list. This does not need to be exhaustive at this stage, but it should be specific.

Eligibility Criteria: e.g., “Adults aged 40-75 with no prior history of CVD.”
Treatment Strategies: e.g., “Initiate a statin within 30 days of the index date” vs. “Do not initiate a statin.”
Outcome: e.g., “Incidence of myocardial infarction or stroke within 5 years of follow-up.”




6. Proposed Causal Method(s)

In one paragraph, state the primary causal method you intend to use to estimate the effect (e.g., propensity score weighting, g-computation). Briefly explain why this method is appropriate for your question and data structure. Mention any key diagnostics you plan to perform (e.g., covariate balance checks).

title: How To Find a Dataset for Target Trial Emulation
text:
Welcome to the data exploration hub for your final project. Finding the right dataset is arguably the most important step in a successful causal inference study. A good dataset doesn’t just have interesting variables; it must have the right structure to allow for the emulation of a target trial.
This page provides you with two things: a powerful tool for searching broadly and a curated list of datasets that are known to be well-suited for this kind of work.

title: How To Find a Dataset for Target Trial Emulation
section: The Go-To Tool: Google Dataset Search
text:
The Go-To Tool: Google Dataset Search
Think of this as Google Scholar, but for data. The Google Dataset Search engine indexes thousands of data repositories from around the world. It is the best place to start when you have a specific topic in mind.
Launch Google Dataset Search 

Tips for Effective Searching
When searching, use keywords that describe the structure of the data you need, not just the topic. Good causal inference requires data where time is well-defined.

Combine your topic (e.g., “cancer”, “education”, “air pollution”) with structural keywords like:
“longitudinal study”
“cohort study”
“prospective data”
“panel data”
“linked mortality data”

title: How To Find a Dataset for Target Trial Emulation
section: Curated Datasets for Target Trial Emulation
text:
Curated Datasets for Target Trial Emulation
Not all datasets are created equal. The best datasets for TTE are longitudinal cohort studies, where a group of people is enrolled at a baseline point in time and followed forward. This structure allows us to properly define eligibility, measure confounders before treatment, and follow individuals for the outcome.
Here are a few high-quality, publicly-available datasets that are exceptionally well-suited for your project.

Framingham Heart Study

Why it’s great for TTE: This is the archetypal prospective cohort study. A cohort of residents from Framingham, MA, was enrolled in 1948 and has been followed ever since. It contains detailed baseline measurements of potential confounders (e.g., smoking, cholesterol, blood pressure) and tracks cardiovascular outcomes over many decades. It’s a perfect dataset for emulating a trial of an intervention (e.g., lifestyle change, medication) on heart disease.
Access: Data is available to researchers through a proposal process. Visit the Framingham Heart Study Website.



MIMIC-IV (Medical Information Mart for Intensive Care)

Why it’s great for TTE: This database of ICU admissions contains high-resolution, time-stamped data. This is critical because you can precisely define time zero (e.g., time of admission, time of a specific diagnosis). Treatments (medications, ventilators) and outcomes are all logged with precise timing, allowing you to emulate a trial of a clinical intervention in a critical care setting and avoid biases like immortal time bias.
Access: Requires completion of a human subjects research training course. Visit the MIMIC-IV Website.



Add Health (The National Longitudinal Study of Adolescent to Adult Health)

Why it’s great for TTE: This is a classic longitudinal cohort. A representative sample of U.S. adolescents was enrolled in 1994-95 and has been followed into adulthood. This is ideal for questions where the “treatment” occurs in adolescence (e.g., participation in sports, a specific educational program) and the outcome occurs in adulthood (e.g., income, health status). The baseline wave contains rich data on potential confounders (family background, school environment, etc.).
Access: Public-use data is readily available. Visit the Add Health Website.



NHANES (National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey) with Linked Mortality Data

Why it’s great for TTE: By itself, NHANES is a series of cross-sectional surveys. However, participants can be linked to the National Death Index. This transforms the dataset into a prospective cohort study. You can use the rich survey data at baseline (diet, lab values, lifestyle) to define eligibility and measure confounders. You can then emulate a trial where the outcome is long-term mortality.
Access: Data is publicly available from the CDC. Visit the NHANES Website.

title: How To Find a Dataset for Target Trial Emulation
text:
✅ Checklist for Evaluating a Dataset
When you find a dataset that looks promising, use this checklist to assess its suitability for a Target Trial Emulation project.

Can you define a clear time zero? Is there a variable that marks the start of follow-up for all individuals (e.g., date of enrollment, date of diagnosis, start of the school year)?
Are confounders measured at or before time zero? The fundamental requirement for confounding control is that your covariates are measured before the treatment is assigned.
Is the exposure/treatment variable well-defined? Can you clearly determine who is “treated” and “untreated” based on the data?
Is the outcome measured after time zero? The dataset must have follow-up data to ascertain the outcome after the intervention.
Is the follow-up period long enough? Is there sufficient time between treatment and outcome for a causal effect to plausibly occur?

If you can answer “yes” to these questions, you likely have a strong candidate dataset for your project.

title: Week 13: Target Trial Emulation
text:
Welcome, class, to STAT 579. We begin our journey into causal inference with what I consider the single most important conceptual tool for applied research: the Target Trial framework (Hernán et al., 2016).
In your statistical training so far, you have become experts at quantifying associations. You can build complex models to predict \(Y\) from \(A\). This course, however, is about a fundamentally different question: “What is the causal effect of \(A\) on \(Y\)?”
The central idea of the target trial framework is simple: every observational analysis that aims to estimate a causal effect is, implicitly, an emulation of a hypothetical, pragmatic randomized trial. This hypothetical, ideal experiment is what we call the “target trial.”
Why start here? Because this framework is the foundational thinking process that must precede any statistical analysis. Before you run a single regression or calculate a single weight, you must first design the experiment you wish you could have run.
By explicitly designing this target trial before you analyze your observational data, you create a clear blueprint. This blueprint serves two critical purposes:

It clarifies your causal question. A vague question like “what is the effect of aspirin?” becomes a precise, answerable question: “What is the 5-year risk of death if individuals with colon cancer initiate daily aspirin 1-month post-surgery, compared with the 5-year risk if they do not initiate aspirin?”
It protects you from common, severe biases. As we will see, many infamous biases in observational research, such as immortal time bias, are “self-inflicted injuries” (Hernán et al. (2016)). They are not inherent to the data but are created by a flawed analysis plan. Explicitly emulating a target trial protocol prevents these errors.

In this lecture, we will define the seven key components of a target trial protocol, distinguish between the two key causal questions (ITT vs. PP), and use this framework to design and critique observational studies.

title: Week 13: Target Trial Emulation
text:
Learning Objectives
By the end of this session, you will be able to:

Define the “target trial” framework and articulate its role as a unifying structure for designing and critiquing observational research.
Identify and explain the seven essential components of a target trial protocol (Eligibility Criteria, Treatment Strategies, Assignment Procedure, Follow-up Period, Outcome, Causal Contrast, and Analysis Plan).
Differentiate between the Intention-to-Treat (ITT) effect and the Per-Protocol (PP) effect as two distinct and valid causal contrasts, and explain the different causal questions they answer.
Explain why a “naïve” per-protocol analysis (e.g., comparing only the adherers in a trial) is biased, using causal diagrams and the concept of post-randomization confounding.
Recognize and diagnose common and severe emulation failures related to Time Zero misalignment, including immortal time bias and prevalent user bias.
Propose valid emulation strategies (e.g., new-user design, grace periods) to address common challenges in observational data.

title: Week 13: Target Trial Emulation
text:
1. Comprehensive Topic Explanation

1.1 The Central Problem: Association vs. Causation
From our first lecture (and Hernán & Robins (2020), Chapter 1), we know that the fundamental challenge of causal inference is that association is not causation.

Association is what we observe in the data. It’s a comparison of different people in different groups.

\(\text{Association} = \E{Y|A=1} - \E{Y|A=0}\)

Causation is what we want to know. It’s a “what if” comparison of the same population under two different scenarios.

\(\text{Causation} = \E{Y^{a=1}} - \E{Y^{a=0}}\)


In the heart transplant example, the association was \(0.11\) (transplant recipients had a higher risk of death), but the causal effect was \(0\). The difference was confounding: sicker patients (\(L=1\)) were both more likely to get a transplant (\(L \to A\)) and more likely to die (\(L \to Y\)).


1.2 The “Gold Standard”: The Randomized Controlled Trial (RCT)
The RCT is our conceptual “gold standard” because it provides a clear path to causal inference. By randomly assigning a treatment strategy \(Z\), an RCT achieves two critical goals:

Breaks Confounding: Random assignment \(Z\) is, by definition, not caused by any patient characteristic (measured \(L\) or unmeasured \(U\)). This breaks all backdoor paths between assignment and outcome.
Defines a Clear Intervention: The trial protocol explicitly defines the treatment strategies being compared.

Visually, randomization severs the link between any confounders (\(L\) or \(U\)) and the intervention, \(Z\).






Figure 1: Left (Observational study): an unmeasured confounder \(U\) (dashed arrows) affects both treatment \(A\) and outcome \(Y\), opening the backdoor path A <- U -> Y \(A \leftarrow U \rightarrow Y\); therefore a simple contrast \(\E{Y|A=1} − \E{Y|A=0}\) is generally biased. Right (Randomized trial): assignment \(Z\) is randomized and thus not caused by \(U\), so the intention‑to‑treat (ITT) effect of assignment (\(Z \to Y\)) is unconfounded (no backdoor \(Z ← U → Y\)). Caveat: adherence A can still be influenced by \(U\) (dashed arrow to \(A\) on the right), so the per‑protocol contrast comparing \(A=1\) vs \(A=0\) may remain confounded by \(U\) and requires additional adjustment or g‑methods to estimate. Dashed arrows indicate unmeasured (latent) variables.



In the RCT (right), the Intention-to-Treat (ITT) effect, which is the causal effect of assignment (\(Z\)) on the outcome (\(Y\)), is unconfounded because the backdoor path \(Z \leftarrow U \to Y\) is broken.


1.3 The Unifying Idea: The Target Trial Framework
Most observational studies are attempts to answer a causal question. The target trial framework formalizes this by stating that every observational analysis should be seen as an emulation of a hypothetical, pragmatic randomized trial.
If we fail to emulate the trial correctly, we introduce biases on top of the usual confounding. By explicitly designing the target trial first, we can avoid these “self-inflicted injuries”.


1.4 The Seven Protocol Components
To design our observational study “as if” it were a trial, we must explicitly specify the seven components of the target trial’s protocol. We will use the example of estimating the effect of aspirin on mortality after colon cancer surgery, as described in Hernán et al. (2016).

1. Eligibility Criteria

What it is: The set of rules that define who is included in the trial.
Rationale: This defines the population to which our causal effect estimate will apply (i.e., its generalizability or transportability). It also ensures that all participants are able to initiate either of the treatment strategies being compared.
Target Trial Example: “Individuals with a new diagnosis of colon cancer, no prior aspirin use, and no contraindications, who survived 1 month post-surgery”.
Observational Emulation Challenge: We must apply these same criteria to our observational data. A common failure is prevalent user bias, where we include people already on aspirin. This is a form of selection bias, as it excludes those who may have tried aspirin and stopped (perhaps due to side effects) or who died shortly after initiation. The correct approach is a new-user design, where we only include individuals at the moment they first become eligible to initiate a strategy.



2. Treatment Strategies

What it is: The interventions we wish to compare. These must be precisely defined and sustained over the follow-up.
Rationale: A vague question like “the effect of aspirin” is ill-defined. We must specify which aspirin strategy (e.g., dose, timing, duration).
Target Trial Example:

Strategy \(g_1\): “Initiate daily aspirin (81mg) at \(T_0\) and continue daily, unless a contraindication or toxicity arises.”
Strategy \(g_0\): “Do not initiate aspirin at \(T_0\) and do not start during follow-up.”

Observational Emulation Challenge: We must find individuals in our data whose observed actions map to these strategies. Note that \(g_1\) is a dynamic strategy: the treatment at time \(k\) depends on a time-varying covariate (toxicity).



3. Assignment Procedure

What it is: The method used to assign individuals to a treatment strategy.
Rationale: This is the core of the causal inference.
Target Trial Example: Randomization at \(T_0\). This ensures the groups are exchangeable (comparable) at baseline. \(Z \indep (Y^a, L, U)\).
Observational Emulation Challenge: This is the one component we cannot replicate. Instead, we must assume conditional exchangeability (or “no unmeasured confounding”). We assume that, conditional on the measured baseline confounders \(L\) (age, disease history, etc.), assignment to the aspirin strategy is “as if” random. We then use adjustment methods (matching, weighting, etc.) to emulate randomization.



4. Follow-up

What it is: When follow-up starts and ends.
Rationale: This must be precisely aligned with assignment and eligibility to avoid bias.
Target Trial Example: Follow-up must start at Time Zero (\(T_0\))—the moment of randomization. It ends at a pre-specified time (e.g., 5 years) or when the outcome occurs (e.g., death).
Observational Emulation Challenge: Our observational follow-up must also start at Time Zero—the moment eligibility is met and the treatment strategy is conceptually assigned (e.g., at 1-month post-surgery). Any misalignment of \(T_0\) with eligibility and assignment leads to bias (see Section 2.1).



5. Outcome

What it is: What is being measured, and how.
Rationale: Must be defined clearly and ascertained consistently across groups.
Target Trial Example: “All-cause mortality within 5 years”.
Observational Emulation Challenge: We must ascertain the outcome (e.g., death from a national registry) in the same way for both groups to avoid differential measurement bias.



6. Causal Contrast (Estimand)

What it is: The specific causal question we are asking.
Rationale: We must decide if we care about the effect of assignment or the effect of adherence. These are two different causal questions.
Target Trial Example:

Intention-to-Treat (ITT) Effect: The causal effect of assignment to the strategies at \(T_0\), regardless of subsequent adherence.
Per-Protocol (PP) Effect: The causal effect of adhering to the strategies for the entire follow-up.

Observational Emulation Challenge: We must also choose.

ITT-analog: Effect of initiation at \(T_0\).
PP-analog: Effect of adherence over time. This is more complex as it involves time-varying treatments.




7. Analysis Plan

What it is: The statistical method used to estimate the chosen causal contrast.
Rationale: The method must match the causal contrast and assumptions.
Target Trial (ITT): Unadjusted (or baseline-adjusted) comparison of risks/rates (e.g., Kaplan-Meier curves, risk ratio).
Observational Emulation (ITT-analog): An adjusted comparison (e.g., matching, IP weighting) to account for baseline confounding.
Observational Emulation (PP-analog): A g-method (e.g., IP weighting of a marginal structural model, g-formula) to account for time-varying confounding.

title: Week 13: Target Trial Emulation
text:
2. Intuitive Clarifications of Challenging Ideas

2.1 The Peril of Misaligned Time Zero (\(T_0\))
The most common “self-inflicted injury” in observational research is failing to align \(T_0\) (the start of follow-up) with eligibility and treatment assignment (Hernán et al., 2016).
Imagine \(T_0\) as the starting line of a race.

Target Trial (Correct): An official (randomization) tells everyone who is eligible (e.g., “no injuries”) to line up at the starting line (\(T_0\)). They are assigned a strategy (“run fast” vs. “run slow”). The official fires a gun, and everyone starts the race (follow-up) at that exact moment.
Observational Emulation (Flawed): We are watching a marathon that has already started.







WarningEmulation Failure 1: Prevalent User Bias



The Error: We start our study at the 10-mile mark. Our \(T_0\) is 10 miles into the race. We compare the people already wearing the “fast shoes” (prevalent users) to those in “slow shoes”.
The Bias: This is selection bias. The only people we see in the “fast shoes” group are those who survived the first 10 miles (i.e., didn’t get a cramp, quit, or collapse). We have selected a biased sample of “survivors” of the early effects of the shoes. This bias is particularly problematic if the treatment has short-term harms.
The Fix: A new-user design. We must stand at the real starting line (\(T_0\)) and only include people as they initiate their strategy.








WarningEmulation Failure 4: Immortal Time Bias



The Error: We stand at the starting line (\(T_0\)). We fire the gun. We wait until the 10-mile mark and then we assign people to groups: “Fast Shoe Group” (if they are wearing fast shoes at 10 miles) vs. “Slow Shoe Group” (all others).
The Bias: This is a severe, self-inflicted bias. The “Fast Shoe Group” by definition had to survive the first 10 miles (the “immortal time”) to even be included in their group. This guarantees they will look better than the “Slow Shoe Group,” which includes all the people who dropped out at mile 6. This is a form of selection bias where we condition on survival.
The Fix: Align assignment with \(T_0\). Classify people into “Fast Shoe Strategy” vs. “Slow Shoe Strategy” based only on the shoes they are wearing at the \(T_0\) starting line (or, more realistically, that they initiate wearing at \(T_0\)).




2.2 The Two Key Causal Questions: ITT vs. PP
This is a major point of confusion from Hernán & Robins (2020) (Chapter 22). Both are valid causal contrasts, but they answer different questions by contrasting different interventions.
Let \(Z\) be the assigned strategy (what the doctor/randomization tells you to do) and \(\overline{A}\) be the received strategy (what you actually do).

1. The Intention-to-Treat (ITT) Effect

Causal Question: What is the causal effect of assignment to a strategy?
Intervention: \(Z=1\) (“Assign to \(g_1\)”) vs. \(Z=0\) (“Assign to \(g_0\)”).
Causal Contrast: \(\E{Y^{z=1}} - \E{Y^{z=0}}\)
Plain English: “What is the 5-year mortality risk if we assign everyone to the aspirin strategy, versus if we assign everyone to the no-aspirin strategy?”
Key Feature: This is a pragmatic or policy-level question. It answers: “What will happen if we implement a program that encourages everyone to take aspirin?” It already accounts for the fact that in the real world, people are not perfectly adherent.
Identification in an RCT: Because \(Z\) is randomized, \(Z\) is unconfounded. We can estimate this directly: \(\E{Y|Z=1} - \E{Y|Z=0}\) (assuming no loss to follow-up).



2. The Per-Protocol (PP) Effect

Causal Question: What is the causal effect of adhering to a strategy?
Intervention: \(\overline{a}=\overline{g}_1\) (“Receive \(g_1\)”) vs. \(\overline{a}=\overline{g}_0\) (“Receive \(g_0\)”).
Causal Contrast: \(\E{Y^{\overline{a}=\overline{g}_1}} - \E{Y^{\overline{a}=\overline{g}_0}}\)
Plain English: “What is the 5-year mortality risk if everyone actually took aspirin as prescribed, versus if everyone actually took no aspirin as prescribed?”
Key Feature: This is the effect of the treatment itself. It’s what a patient who plans to adhere wants to know.
Identification in an RCT: This is hard! We cannot just compare the people who happened to adhere (the “naïve per-protocol” analysis).
Why is the “naïve” analysis biased? Adherence (\(\overline{A}\)) is a post-randomization behavior. It is confounded by factors (\(L_k, U_k\)) like side effects or new symptoms, which themselves predict the outcome \(Y\). This creates treatment-confounder feedback and selection bias.
Conclusion: To estimate the PP effect, we must treat the RCT (or our observational study) as an observational study of a time-varying treatment and adjust for the time-varying confounders that predict adherence. This is why we need the g-methods from Part III.


Comparison of the Intention-to-Treat (ITT) Effect vs. the Per-Protocol (PP) Effect.{#tbl-itt-vs-pp}

title: Week 13: Target Trial Emulation
text:
3. Simple, Hand-Calculation Numerical Example(s)

Example 1: Diagnosing Immortal Time Bias (Failure 4)
Let’s use a simple example to see the bias in action.

Goal: Does Drug A reduce 1-year mortality?
Data: 100 patients. 50 die at 6 months. 50 survive the full 12 months.
Incorrect Design:

\(T_0\) = Study start.
“Treated Group” (\(A=1\)): Defined as those who survive at least 9 months and are taking the drug at 9 months.
“Untreated Group” (\(A=0\)): All others.

Analysis:

The 50 patients who died at 6 months cannot be in the “Treated Group” because they didn’t survive to 9 months. They are all, by definition, in the “Untreated Group”.
The 50 patients who survived 12 months are the only ones eligible for the “Treated Group”. Let’s say 25 of them took the drug for >9 months (so they land in \(A=1\)) and 25 did not (so they land in \(A=0\)).

Calculate the Biased Risk:

Risk (Treated, \(A=1\)):

N = 25 (the survivors who took the drug).
Deaths = 0 (they all survived 12 months).
Risk = 0 / 25 = 0%

Risk (Untreated, \(A=0\)):

N = 75 (the 50 who died early + the 25 survivors who didn’t take the drug).
Deaths = 50 (the 50 who died early).
Risk = 50 / 75 = 66.7%


Biased Conclusion: The drug appears to be miraculously effective (Risk Ratio = 0). The bias comes from the 9 months of “immortal time” we guaranteed for the treated group.



Example 2: Diagnosing Prevalent User Bias (Failure 1)

Goal: Does Drug A prevent 1-year mortality?
Data: We recruit 100 patients on Jan 1, 2024. This is our \(T_0\).
Incorrect Design:

We define our groups based on their drug use at \(T_0\).
“Treated Group” (\(A=1\)): 50 patients who are already taking Drug A on Jan 1 (prevalent users).
“Untreated Group” (\(A=0\)): 50 patients who are not taking Drug A on Jan 1.

The Unseen Problem: The drug has a dangerous side effect: 10% of people who initiate it die within the first month. In 2023, 55 people started the drug. 5 died, leaving the 50 “healthy survivors” we see in our \(A=1\) group. The 50 people in our \(A=0\) group are just the general population.
Calculate the Biased Risk:

Assume the “baseline” 1-year risk for everyone is 20%.
Risk (Treated, \(A=1\)):

N = 50. These are “healthy survivors” of the initial risk. Let’s say their 1-year risk is now only 10% (5 deaths).
Risk = 5 / 50 = 10%

Risk (Untreated, \(A=0\)):

N = 50. These are the general population. Their risk is 20% (10 deaths).
Risk = 10 / 50 = 20%


Biased Conclusion: The drug looks protective (RR = 0.5). We’ve introduced selection bias by only including the “prevalent users” who were healthy enough to survive the initial high-risk period.

title: Week 13: Target Trial Emulation
text:
4. R Code Examples & Interpretation
Let’s use dagitty and ggdag to visualize the causal structures for our key concepts.

1. DAG: ITT vs. Naïve Per-Protocol in an RCT
In an RCT, the ITT effect (\(Z \to \dots \to Y\)) is unconfounded. But the PP effect (\(A \to Y\)) is confounded by \(U\) (e.g., frailty, motivation) which affects both adherence (\(A\)) and outcome (\(Y\)). A “naïve” analysis that just compares \(A=1\) to \(A=0\) will be biased by the open backdoor path \(A \leftarrow U \to Y\).






Figure 2: DAG for an RCT. The ITT effect (\(Z \to Y\)) is unconfounded. The green arrow indicates the ITT effect of assignment (it is not a direct effect of \(Z\) on \(Y\), but goes through \(A\)). The PP effect (\(A \to Y\)) is confounded by \(U\). Note that the red arrow indicates the causal effect of interest for the PP analysis, while the blue dashed arrows indicate confounding paths.





2. DAG: Per-Protocol Emulation with Time-Varying Confounding
This is the key challenge for estimating the PP effect. To get the effect of the full strategy (\(A_0, A_1\)) on \(Y\), we must adjust for \(L_0\) and \(L_1\). But \(L_1\) (e.g., a side effect) is caused by \(A_0\).
This creates treatment-confounder feedback. As we see, \(L_1\) is:

A confounder for the \(A_1 \to Y\) effect (it opens the backdoor path \(A_1 \leftarrow L_1 \to Y\)).
A mediator for the \(A_0 \to Y\) effect (it is on the causal path \(A_0 \to L_1 \to Y\)).

Standard regression adjustment for \(L_1\) would block part of the \(A_0\) effect and (as we’ll see in Ch. 20) can introduce selection bias. This is why we need g-methods.






Figure 3: Target trial emulation with treatment-confounder feedback. \(L_1\) is a time-varying confounder for the \(A1 \to Y\) effect that is also affected by past treatment \(A_0\).

title: Week 13: Target Trial Emulation
text:
5. Hands-On R Lab
STAT 579: R Lab 2 Emulating a Target Trial: Aspirin & Mortality

Lab Objectives

Simulate a “messy” observational dataset that includes baseline confounders and time-to-event data.
Perform a biased analysis using a design that fails to emulate the target trial (Emulation Failure 4: Immortal Time Bias).
Perform a correct emulation of the target trial by:

Defining eligibility at time zero.
Assigning treatment strategies at time zero (using a grace period).
Starting follow-up at time zero.

Adjust for baseline confounding in the emulated trial using a regression model.
Compare and interpret the results from the biased and correct analyses.



1. Warm-up & Setup
Reading: Before starting the lab, please review Hernán et al. (2016), sections 2 and 3.
Warm-up Questions (Discuss with a partner):

What are the 7 components of the aspirin target trial described in Section 2 of the paper?
What is “immortal time”? How does Emulation Failure 4 (Fig 1) guarantee that the treated group will have a “period… during which the risk is guaranteed to be exactly zero”?

First, let’s load our packages and set a random seed for reproducibility.


Code
pacman::p_load(tidyverse, survival, lubridate, gtsummary)
set.seed(1989) # For reproducibility




2. Simulate “Messy” Observational Data
We will simulate a “raw” dataset of 2,000 patients who had colon cancer surgery. This represents the messy electronic medical record (EMR) data we get before applying our target trial design.

U_frailty is an unmeasured “healthy/frail” status. Healthy (\(U=0\)) patients are more likely to take aspirin and less likely to die. This is our unmeasured confounder.
age and history_chd are our measured confounders (\(L\)).
Aspirin initiation can happen any time after surgery.
Death can happen any time after surgery.



Code
n <- 2000
dat_raw <- tibble(
  id = 1:n,
  # U: Unmeasured confounder
  U_frailty = rbinom(n, 1, 0.4), # 40% are frail

  # L: Measured confounders
  age = rnorm(n, 60, 8),
  history_chd = rbinom(n, 1, 0.2 + U_frailty * 0.2), # Frail more likely to have CHD

  # Surgery Date (our "anchor" event)
  surgery_date = as.Date("2020-01-01") + runif(n, 0, 365),

  # A: Aspirin Initiation
  # Healthy (U=0) and younger patients are more likely to initiate
  prob_asa = plogis(
    -1 - 0.5 * U_frailty + 0.1 * (age - 60) - 0.2 * history_chd
  ),
  initiates_asa = rbinom(n, 1, prob_asa),
  asa_init_date = if_else(
    initiates_asa == 1,
    surgery_date + runif(n, 1, 730), # Initiates 1 day to 2 yrs post-op
    as.Date(NA)
  ),

  # Y: Death
  # We simulate a "true" survival time.
  # Hazard is higher for frail, older, CHD patients
  log_haz_death = -5 + 1.5 * U_frailty + 0.05 * (age - 60) + 0.5 * history_chd,

  # We generate a time-to-death assuming no aspirin
  time_to_death_no_asa = rexp(n, exp(log_haz_death)),

  # True Causal Effect: Aspirin has a Hazard Ratio of 0.7
  time_to_death = if_else(
    initiates_asa == 1,
    time_to_death_no_asa / 0.7,
    time_to_death_no_asa
  ),

  death_date = surgery_date + time_to_death
)

# Clean up raw data
dat_raw <- dat_raw |>
  select(
    id,
    U_frailty,
    age,
    history_chd,
    surgery_date,
    asa_init_date,
    death_date
  )




3. Task 0: Explore the Raw Data
Before any analysis, look at the raw data. Get a feel for the variables.

glimpse(dat_raw)

summary(dat_raw)

# How many people initiated aspirin?
dat_raw |>
  summarise(
    n_total = n(),
    n_initiators = sum(!is.na(asa_init_date)),
    percent_initiators = 100 * (n_initiators / n_total)
  )



4. Task 1: The Biased “Immortal Time” Analysis
Goal: Perform a flawed analysis based on “Emulation Failure 4”.

\(T_0\): 1 month post-surgery (our “anchor”).
Groups:

"Ever Aspirin": Anyone who ever initiated aspirin (even 2 years later).
"Never Aspirin": Anyone who never did.

Follow-up: Start at \(T_0\) for 5 years.


# STUDENT TO FILL IN
dat_biased <- dat_raw |>
  mutate(
    time_zero = surgery_date + months(1), # 1 month after surgery_date

    # Biased group assignment based on *any* future use
    strategy_group = if_else(
      is.na(asa_init_date),
      "Never Aspirin",
      "Ever Aspirin"
    ),

    # Follow-up ends at 5 years (1826 days) post-T0 or at death
    followup_end = time_zero + days(1826),
    time_to_event = as.numeric(
      pmin(death_date, followup_end, na.rm = TRUE) - time_zero
    ),
    status = if_else(!is.na(death_date) & death_date <= followup_end, 1, 0)
  ) |>
  # Filter out anyone who died *before* T0
  dplyr::filter(time_to_event > 0)
s
# Run the Cox model
cox_biased <- coxph(
  Surv(time_to_event, status) ~ strategy_group + age + history_chd,
  data = dat_biased
)

# Display the biased result
tbl_regression(cox_biased, exponentiate = TRUE)

# Display the biased result

5. Task 2: Emulating the Target Trial (Correctly)
Now, let’s follow the target trial protocol. We will align \(T_0\), eligibility, and treatment assignment.

\(T_0\): 1 month post-surgery.
Eligibility: Must be alive at \(T_0\).
Strategies: We’ll use a 3-month (90-day) grace period to make the emulation realistic.

Strategy 1 (Aspirin): Initiates aspirin between \(T_0\) and \(T_0 + 90\) days.
Strategy 0 (No Aspirin): Does not initiate aspirin between \(T_0\) and \(T_0 + 90\) days.

Analysis: ITT-analog. We compare the groups as defined at baseline and follow them for 5 years, regardless of what they do after the grace period.


# STUDENT TO FILL IN
dat_tt <- dat_raw |>
  mutate(
    time_zero = `...`,
    followup_end = `...`,

    # Define strategy assignment *at T0* (using a 90-day grace period)
    asa_within_grace = !is.na(asa_init_date) &
      asa_init_date >= `...` &
      asa_init_date <= (`...` + days(90)),

    strategy_group = if_else(
      asa_within_grace == TRUE,
      "Aspirin Strategy",
      "No Aspirin Strategy"
    ),

    # Define outcome and follow-up time *from T0*
    time_to_event = as.numeric(pmin(`...`, `...`, na.rm = TRUE) - `...`),
    status = if_else(!is.na(`...`) & `...` <= `...`, 1, 0)
  ) |>
  # Apply eligibility criteria AT T0
  dplyr::filter(time_to_event > 0) # Must be alive at T0

# Run the Cox model, adjusting for baseline confounders
cox_tt <- coxph(
  Surv(time_to_event, status) ~ strategy_group + age + history_chd,
  data = dat_tt
)

# Display the target trial emulation result
tbl_regression(cox_tt, exponentiate = TRUE)

title: Week 13: Target Trial Emulation
text:
6. Common Pitfalls & Checks






WarningCommon Pitfall: Misaligned Time Zero



The single biggest mistake in observational studies of sustained treatments is misaligning \(T_0\). The Hernán et al. (2016) paper gives 4 classic examples. Always check your (or others’) analyses for these:

Failure 1 (Prevalent User Bias): \(T_0\) is after strategy assignment.

Example: Study of statins and dementia. \(T_0\) is age 65. “Treated” group are those taking statins at age 65.
Bias: Selection bias. You miss everyone who tried statins and quit (maybe due to side effects) and everyone who died before 65 (maybe due to the statin).
Fix: A new-user design. We must stand at the real starting line (\(T_0\)) and only include people as they initiate their strategy.

Failure 2 (Eligibility after \(T_0\)): \(T_0\) is at eligibility, but after strategy assignment.

Example: Study of aspirin. \(T_0\) is 1-month post-surgery (eligibility). But the “treated” group is defined as those who started aspirin before surgery.
Bias: Selection bias. The “treated” group is selected on surviving until \(T_0\).

Failure 3 (Immortal Time before Eligibility): \(T_0\) is before eligibility is fully met.

Example: Study of post-surgery aspirin. \(T_0\) is the date of cancer diagnosis. “Treated” is defined as starting aspirin at diagnosis.
Bias: Immortal time. The outcome (death) can’t happen between \(T_0\) (diagnosis) and the end of eligibility (1-month post-surgery).

Failure 4 (Immortal Time after \(T_0\)): \(T_0\) is at eligibility, but strategy is assigned later.

Example: Our hand-calculation and lab example. \(T_0\) is 1-month post-surgery. “Treated” is defined as “used aspirin for \(\ge 6\) months.”
Bias: Immortal time. The treated group is guaranteed to be alive and in follow-up for at least 6 months.

title: Week 13: Target Trial Emulation
text:
Check Your Understanding

Question: An analyst wants to study the effect of statins on heart attacks. They define the “treated” group as anyone who filled \(\ge 2\) statin prescriptions and the “control” group as anyone who filled 0. They start follow-up for everyone at Jan 1, 2020. A patient who dies on Jan 15, 2020 (and filled 0 prescriptions) is put in the control group. What bias is this?


Answer: This is classic immortal time bias (Emulation Failure 4). The “treated” group is guaranteed to be immortal for the time it takes to fill 2 prescriptions, while the “control” group includes people who die early.


Question: What is the only way to correctly estimate a per-protocol effect in a trial with non-adherence and time-varying prognostic factors (e.g., factors that predict both adherence and the outcome)?


Answer: You must use a method that can handle time-varying treatment-confounder feedback, such as the g-methods (IP weighting, g-formula, g-estimation).


Question: You are emulating a target trial. You find that many people in your observational data don’t start their assigned “aspirin” strategy exactly at \(T_0\), but rather 2-3 months later. If you exclude them, what bias might you introduce? What is a better approach?


Answer: Excluding them could introduce selection bias if the reasons for their delay are related to the outcome. A better approach is to specify a grace period (e.g., 3 months) in your target trial protocol. This defines the “Aspirin Strategy” as “initiating within 3 months”. This makes the emulation more realistic and increases the number of eligible individuals.

title: Week 13: Target Trial Emulation
text:
Appendix: Advanced Theory & Derivations

Formalizing the ITT and Per-Protocol Estimands
Let’s formalize the concepts from Section 2. We use the potential outcomes framework from Hernán & Robins (2020) (Chapter 22).

Let \(Z_i\) be the randomized assignment for individual \(i\) at \(T_0\).

\(Z=1\): Assigned to “strategy \(g_1\)” (e.g., take aspirin).
\(Z=0\): Assigned to “strategy \(g_0\)” (e.g., no aspirin).

Let \(\overline{A}_i = (A_{i,0}, A_{i,1}, \dots, A_{i,K})\) be the received treatment history.
Let \(Y_i\) be the observed outcome.


The Intention-to-Treat (ITT) Effect
The ITT effect is the causal effect of assignment.

Potential Outcomes:

\(Y_i^{z=1}\): The outcome for individual \(i\) if they had been assigned to strategy \(g_1\).
\(Y_i^{z=0}\): The outcome for individual \(i\) if they had been assigned to strategy \(g_0\).

Causal Contrast (Estimand):

\[
ACE_{ITT} = \E{Y^{z=1}} - \E{Y^{z=0}}
\]

Identification: By randomization, assignment \(Z_i\) is independent of the potential outcomes: \((Y_i^{z=1}, Y_i^{z=0}) \indep Z_i\). This is exchangeability.
Result: Because of exchangeability, \(\E{Y^{z}} = \E{Y|Z=z}\). Therefore, the causal ITT effect is identified by the simple associational contrast:

\[
ACE_{ITT} = \E{Y | Z=1} - \E{Y | Z=0}
\]
This holds assuming no loss to follow-up (selection bias).


The Per-Protocol (PP) Effect
The PP effect is the causal effect of adhering to the strategies.

Potential Outcomes: Let \(\overline{g}_1\) and \(\overline{g}_0\) be the full treatment histories specified in the protocol (e.g., \(g_1\) = “take aspirin daily for 5 years”, \(g_0\) = “take no aspirin for 5 years”).

\(Y_i^{\overline{a}=\overline{g}_1}\): The outcome for individual \(i\) if they had perfectly adhered to strategy \(g_1\).
\(Y_i^{\overline{a}=\overline{g}_0}\): The outcome for individual \(i\) if they had perfectly adhered to strategy \(g_0\).

Causal Contrast (Estimand):

\[
ACE_{PP} = \E{Y^{\overline{a}=\overline{g}_1}} - \E{Y^{\overline{a}=\overline{g}_0}}
\]

Identification Challenge: This is not identified by a simple associational contrast, even in an RCT.
The “Naïve” Analysis (BIAS): The analysis that compares \(\E{Y | \overline{A} = \overline{g}_1}\) vs. \(\E{Y | \overline{A} = \overline{g}_0}\) is confounded.
Why? \(\overline{A}\) (received treatment) is a post-randomization behavior. Unmeasured factors \(U\) (like frailty, motivation) can affect both whether a person adheres (\(\overline{A}\)) and their outcome (\(Y\)). This creates a confounding path: \(\overline{A} \leftarrow U \to Y\).
Result: To estimate the PP effect, we must treat the RCT as an observational study. We must assume sequential exchangeability conditional on the measured time-varying covariates \(L_k\) (e.g., symptoms, side effects) that predict adherence. We must then use g-methods (IP weighting, g-formula) to adjust for this time-varying confounding.




Formalizing “Cloning” for Complex Assignment
In Section 2.2, we discussed two problems: (1) individuals being eligible for multiple strategies at \(T_0\), and (2) grace periods. Both are solved by “cloning” (Hernán & Robins, 2020, Chapter 22).

The Problem: At \(T_0\), an individual (e.g., \(L_0=0\)) is eligible for both strategy \(g_1\) (“start when \(L_1=1\)”) and strategy \(g_0\) (“never start”). Their observed data \(\overline{A}\) and \(\overline{L}\) are consistent with both.
The Solution:

Create two “clones” of this individual in the dataset.
Clone 1: Assign to strategy \(g_1\).
Clone 2: Assign to strategy \(g_0\).
Follow both clones over time.
If the real person’s \(L_1\) becomes 1 and they start treatment (\(A_1=1\)), their data are no longer consistent with strategy \(g_0\). We therefore censor Clone 2 at time \(k=1\). Clone 1 continues.
If the real person’s \(L_1\) becomes 1 and they do not start treatment (\(A_1=0\)), their data are no longer consistent with strategy \(g_1\). We therefore censor Clone 1 at time \(k=1\). Clone 2 continues.

The Analysis: This “cloning and censoring” procedure creates a new dataset where assignment is clear at \(T_0\). However, it introduces time-varying censoring that is highly informative (it depends on \(L_k\) and \(A_k\)).
The Result: We must use a g-method (like IP weighting) to handle this induced selection bias. We would create weights \(SW^C\) to account for this censoring, as described in Chapter 21 of Hernán & Robins (2020).

This advanced technique is the formal basis for emulating target trials with complex, dynamic strategies or grace periods.

title: Week 10: Quantitative Bias Analysis, Tipping-Point Logic, and The E-value
text:
Welcome, class. For the past eleven weeks, we have dedicated ourselves to the rigorous estimation of causal effects, primarily focusing on methods to control for measured confounders. We have used regression, matching, stratification, and inverse probability weighting to “close backdoor paths” and emulate a randomized controlled trial (RCT) from observational data.
All of these methods, however, rest on one critical, untestable assumption: conditional exchangeability, or “no unmeasured confounding.” We assume that the set of covariates \(L\) we measured and adjusted for is sufficient to make the exposed and unexposed groups comparable.
This week, we confront the “Achilles’ heel” of observational research head-on. What if our assumption is wrong? What if there is an unmeasured confounder \(U\) that biases our results?
This module introduces sensitivity analysis, a formal method for quantifying the potential impact of unmeasured confounding. We will shift our question from the unanswerable, “Is there unmeasured confounding?” to the answerable, “How strong would an unmeasured confounder have to be to change our conclusion?”
We will focus on a powerful, intuitive, and now standard tool: the E-value (VanderWeele & Ding, 2017). The E-value provides a “tipping point” analysis, helping us gauge the robustness of our findings and fostering a more honest and critical discussion about the limitations of our causal claims.

title: Week 10: Quantitative Bias Analysis, Tipping-Point Logic, and The E-value
text:
Background
Excellent question. This distinction is the absolute core of our work in this course. It’s the difference between what we want to know (the causal effect) and what we can actually calculate from our data (the association).
Let’s define these terms formally.

The True, Causal Risk Ratio (\(RR_{AY}^c\))
This is our causal estimand. It answers the “what if” question.
The true, causal risk ratio compares the risk of the outcome (\(Y=1\)) in an entire population if everyone were exposed (\(a=1\)) to the risk of the outcome in that same population if everyone were unexposed (\(a=0\)).
We define it using potential outcomes (see Chapter 1 of Hernán & Robins (2020)):

Let \(Y^{a=1}\) be the potential outcome for an individual had they, possibly contrary to fact, received the exposure.
Let \(Y^{a=0}\) be the potential outcome for that same individual had they not received the exposure.

The causal risk ratio is the ratio of the population-level probabilities (or risks) of these two potential outcomes:
\[
RR_{AY}^c = \frac{P(Y^{a=1} = 1)}{P(Y^{a=0} = 1)}
\]

The numerator, \(P(Y^{a=1} = 1)\), is the causal risk under exposure.
The denominator, \(P(Y^{a=0} = 1)\), is the causal risk under non-exposure.

Key Idea: This is a comparison of two hypothetical, counterfactual worlds. We can never observe both potential outcomes for the same person at the same time (the “fundamental problem of causal inference”). Our goal in an observational study is to use data to estimate this unobservable quantity.


The Observed, Associational Risk Ratio (\(RR_{AY|L}\))
This is our associational measure. It’s what we actually compute from our observational data after adjusting for a set of measured covariates, \(L\).
The observed, conditional risk ratio compares the risk of the outcome among the exposed to the risk of the outcome among the unexposed, within a specific stratum (or subset) of the population defined by \(L=l\).
We define it using standard conditional probabilities:
\[
RR_{AY|L=l} = \frac{P(Y=1 \mid A=1, L=l)}{P(Y=1 \mid A=0, L=l)}
\]

The numerator, \(P(Y=1 \mid A=1, L=l)\), is the observed risk among the exposed in stratum \(l\).
The denominator, \(P(Y=1 \mid A=0, L=l)\), is the observed risk among the unexposed in that same stratum \(l\).







Note



We often report a single “adjusted” or “standardized” \(RR_{AY|L}\) by averaging these stratum-specific measures, for example, by standardizing them to the population distribution of \(L\) or by using a regression model (e.g., logistic, log-binomial) that assumes a common \(RR\) across strata.




The Crucial Link
In an observational study, we hope that our adjusted associational measure \(RR_{AY|L}\) is a valid estimate of the true causal measure \(RR_{AY}^c\).
This “hope” is our key assumption: conditional exchangeability (or no unmeasured confounding).
If we assume \(Y^a \indep A \mid L\), then the causal risks within a stratum equal the associational risks:

\(P(Y^{a=1} = 1 \mid L=l) = P(Y=1 \mid A=1, L=l)\)
\(P(Y^{a=0} = 1 \mid L=l) = P(Y=1 \mid A=0, L=l)\)

When this holds, our adjusted \(RR_{AY|L}\) identifies the causal \(RR_{AY}^c\). The purpose of sensitivity analysis is to probe what happens when this assumption fails.

title: Week 10: Quantitative Bias Analysis, Tipping-Point Logic, and The E-value
text:
Comprehensive Topic Explanation

The Core Problem: Unmeasured Confounding
All our methods for causal inference from observational data—regression, matching, IPW—rely on the assumption of conditional exchangeability. Formally, given a set of measured covariates \(L\):
\[
Y^a \indep A \mid L
\]
This assumption states that, within strata of \(L\), treatment assignment \(A\) is independent of the potential outcomes \(Y^a\). In DAG terminology, it means our set \(L\) is sufficient to block all non-causal backdoor paths between \(A\) and \(Y\).
The problem is that we can never be certain we have measured all relevant covariates. There may be an unmeasured variable \(U\) (e.g., genetic predisposition, health-seeking behavior, lifestyle factors) that is a common cause of both \(A\) and \(Y\).
Our causal diagram would look like this:






Figure 1: DAG showing unmeasured confounding by \(U\) between exposure \(A\) and outcome \(Y\), with measured covariates \(L\).



If we adjust for \(L\), we successfully block the backdoor path \(A \leftarrow L \rightarrow Y\). However, the path \(A \leftarrow U \rightarrow Y\) remains open, and our effect estimate will be a mix of the true causal effect and bias from this unmeasured confounding.


From “Is there bias?” to “How much bias?”
We cannot use our data to test for the presence of \(U\). This is a fundamental limitation. Data you don’t have cannot be analyzed.
Therefore, we must pivot. Instead of claiming “there is no unmeasured confounding,” we perform a sensitivity analysis. We assume our observed association (e.g., \(RR_{AY|L} = 2.0\)) is biased and ask a “what if” question:

“How strong would an unmeasured confounder \(U\) have to be to fully explain away this observed association?”

“Explain away” means: how strong would the \(U \rightarrow A\) and \(U \rightarrow Y\) relationships need to be to make the true, causal risk ratio \(RR_{AY}^c\) equal to 1.0 (the null)?


The E-value: A Tipping-Point Metric
The E-value provides a direct answer to this question (VanderWeele & Ding, 2017).






Note📖 Definition



The E-value is the minimum strength of association (on the risk ratio scale) that an unmeasured confounder \(U\) would need to have with both the exposure \(A\) and the outcome \(Y\), conditional on the measured covariates \(L\), to reduce the observed risk ratio to 1.0.




Bias Parameters
To formalize this, we define two bias parameters for a (hypothetical, binary) unmeasured confounder \(U\):

\(RR_{AU}\): The risk ratio for the association between the confounder \(U\) and the exposure \(A\).

\(RR_{AU} = \frac{P(A=1 | U=1, L)}{P(A=1 | U=0, L)}\)

\(RR_{UY}\): The risk ratio for the association between the confounder \(U\) and the outcome \(Y\).

\(RR_{UY} = \frac{P(Y=1 | A, U=1, L)}{P(Y=1 | A, U=0, L)}\)


The E-value simplifies this by setting \(RR_{AU} = RR_{UY} = \gamma\) and finding the minimum \(\gamma\) that could “explain away” the effect.


Two Types of E-values
We must consider two distinct “tipping points”:

E-value for the Point Estimate: The minimum \(\gamma\) needed to move the point estimate (e.g., \(RR=2.0\)) to the null (\(RR_c=1.0\)).
E-value for the Confidence Interval: The minimum \(\gamma\) needed to move the confidence interval limit closest to the null (e.g., \(RR=1.2\)) to the null.

As we will see, the E-value for the CI is the more important and conservative metric. It answers the question: “How strong would confounding have to be to make our finding statistically non-significant?”

title: Week 10: Quantitative Bias Analysis, Tipping-Point Logic, and The E-value
text:
Intuitive Clarifications of Challenging Ideas

Analogy: The “Missing Witness” in a Trial
Think of your observational study as a court case. You are the prosecutor, arguing that \(A\) “caused” \(Y\). You present your evidence: an adjusted risk ratio of \(RR=2.5\) (95% CI [1.5, 4.0]).
The defense (a skeptical colleague) argues, “Your finding is just confounding. You forgot to account for \(U\).”
This is like the defense claiming a “missing witness” (\(U\)) would have provided an alibi.

Before the E-value: The argument stops. The prosecutor says “I measured \(L\),” and the defense says “But you didn’t measure \(U\).” We are at an impasse.
With the E-value: The judge (the scientific community) turns to the defense and says, “Okay. If this ‘missing witness’ \(U\) exists, how compelling must their testimony be?”

The E-value calculation tells us: “To acquit the defendant (i.e., make the true effect \(RR_c=1.0\)), the missing witness \(U\) must be a very strong predictor of both the crime (outcome \(Y\)) and the defendant’s presence (exposure \(A\)).”
If the E-value is high (e.g., 5.0), we can say: “This ‘missing witness’ \(U\) would need to be 5-fold associated with both \(A\) and \(Y\). That’s a stronger risk factor than smoking for this exposure! We find that implausible.” This strengthens our case.
If the E-value is low (e.g., 1.5), we must concede: “A ‘missing witness’ \(U\) who is only 1.5-fold associated with \(A\) and \(Y\)—like modest confounding by ‘healthy lifestyle’—could undo our finding. Our case is weak.”

title: Week 10: Quantitative Bias Analysis, Tipping-Point Logic, and The E-value
text:
Simple, Hand-Calculation Numerical Example(s)
The formula for the E-value (for an \(RR_{obs} > 1\)) is surprisingly simple:
\[
E\text{-value} = RR_{obs} + \sqrt{RR_{obs} \times (RR_{obs} - 1)}
\]
If \(RR_{obs} < 1\) (a protective effect), we simply invert it (\(1/RR_{obs}\)) and use the same formula.

title: Week 10: Quantitative Bias Analysis, Tipping-Point Logic, and The E-value
section: Worked Example: Point Estimate and CI
text:
Worked Example: Point Estimate and CI
A (fictional) clinical epidemiology study finds that patients taking a new diabetes drug (\(A\)) have an elevated risk of pancreatitis (\(Y\)). After adjusting for age, sex, BMI, and smoking status (\(L\)), they report:

Adjusted Risk Ratio (\(RR_{obs}\)): 3.0
95% Confidence Interval: [1.8, 5.0]

Let’s calculate the E-values.

1. E-value for the Point Estimate
We use \(RR_{obs} = 3.0\).

Step 1: \(E\text{-value} = 3.0 + \sqrt{3.0 \times (3.0 - 1)}\)
Step 2: \(E\text{-value} = 3.0 + \sqrt{3.0 \times 2.0}\)
Step 3: \(E\text{-value} = 3.0 + \sqrt{6.0}\)
Step 4: \(E\text{-value} \approx 3.0 + 2.45 = \mathbf{5.45}\)

Interpretation: To fully explain away the 3-fold observed increase in risk, an unmeasured confounder \(U\) would need to be associated with both the new drug (\(A\)) and pancreatitis (\(Y\)) by a risk ratio of at least 5.45-fold, conditional on \(L\).


2. E-value for the Confidence Interval
This is the more critical measure. We want to know what it would take to make the finding non-significant, i.e., move the CI to touch 1.0. We must use the CI limit closest to the null.
Here, the lower limit is \(1.8\). We use \(RR_{obs} = 1.8\).

Step 1: \(E\text{-value (CI)} = 1.8 + \sqrt{1.8 \times (1.8 - 1)}\)
Step 2: \(E\text{-value (CI)} = 1.8 + \sqrt{1.8 \times 0.8}\)
Step 3: \(E\text{-value (CI)} = 1.8 + \sqrt{1.44}\)
Step 4: \(E\text{-value (CI)} = 1.8 + 1.2 = \mathbf{3.0}\)

Interpretation: This is the key finding. An unmeasured confounder \(U\) associated with both \(A\) and \(Y\) by a risk ratio of 3.0 would be strong enough to shift the 95% confidence interval to include the null value of 1.0.
We would then ask ourselves: “Is there a plausible confounder (e.g., ‘pre-pancreatic disease state’) that we failed to measure that could increase the risk of receiving this new drug by 3-fold and increase the risk of pancreatitis by 3-fold, even after we’ve adjusted for BMI and smoking?” This is a concrete, debatable question.

title: Week 10: Quantitative Bias Analysis, Tipping-Point Logic, and The E-value
text:
R Code Examples & Interpretation
Calculating the E-value by hand is essential for intuition, but in practice, we use the EValue package.

Example 1: The evalues.RR() Function
Let’s use our hand-calculation example: \(RR = 3.0\) (95% CI [1.8, 5.0]).


Code
# Load the Library
library(EValue)

# Calculate E-value for RR, with Lower (lo) and Upper (hi) CI
results <- evalues.RR(est = 3.0, lo = 1.8, hi = 5.0)

# Print the Results
print(results)


R Output (Simulated):
          point    lower    upper
RR        3.000    1.800    5.000
E-value   5.449    3.000       NA
Interpretation:

The output provides the E-value for the point estimate (point: 5.449) and the E-value for the CI limit closest to the null (lower: 3.000).
The NA for the upper bound is correct; we don’t care how much bias is needed to explain away the upper limit, only the one closest to the null.
Our hand-calculations are confirmed! The E-value for the point estimate is 5.45, and the E-value for the CI is 3.0.



Example 2: Protective Effects
What about a study finding a protective effect? A (fictional) study suggests moderate coffee consumption (\(A\)) reduces the 10-year risk of dementia (\(Y\)).

Adjusted Risk Ratio (\(RR_{obs}\)): 0.80
95% Confidence Interval: [0.70, 0.92]

The evalues.RR function handles this automatically.


Code
# The Function Knows that an RR < 1 is Protective
# It Will Automatically Calculate E-values for 1/RR
protective_results <- evalues.RR(est = 0.80, lo = 0.70, hi = 0.92)

print(protective_results)


R Output (Simulated):
          point    lower    upper
RR        0.800    0.700    0.920
E-value   1.809       NA    1.319
Interpretation:

Notice the E-values are now calculated for the inverted RRs.

Point estimate: \(RR = 1/0.80 = 1.25\). E-value = \(1.25 + \sqrt{1.25(0.25)} \approx 1.81\).
CI limit: \(RR = 1/0.92 \approx 1.087\). E-value = \(1.087 + \sqrt{1.087(0.087)} \approx 1.32\).

The E-value for the CI is 1.32 (on the upper column, as \(1/0.92\) is the CI limit closest to the null).
Conclusion: This finding is highly sensitive to unmeasured confounding. A confounder \(U\) (e.g., “higher socioeconomic status”) that is associated with drinking coffee by 1.32-fold and also associated with reduced dementia risk by 1.32-fold would be sufficient to make this finding statistically non-significant. This is a very plausible level of confounding.

title: Week 10: Quantitative Bias Analysis, Tipping-Point Logic, and The E-value
text:
Hands-On R Lab

Week 12 R Lab: Quantifying Robustness with E-values
Objective: To practice calculating and, more importantly, interpreting E-values from a simulated study finding.
Lab Warm-Up (Flipped Design): Before starting this lab, please answer the following:

Read Chapter 19 from Hernán & Robins (2020).
In your own words, what is the key difference between an E-value for a point estimate and an E-value for a confidence interval?
Why is the latter (for the CI) the more important metric for researchers?



Lab Scenario
You are a biostatistician collaborating on an observational study of a new anti-hypertensive medication (let’s call it “Drug X”). The team followed 10,000 patients for 5 years to see if Drug X (\(A=1\)) reduced the risk of stroke (\(Y=1\)) compared to standard care (\(A=0\)).
After adjusting for a rich set of measured covariates \(L\) (age, sex, baseline blood pressure, diabetes status, smoking), the final model produced the following:

Adjusted Risk Ratio (\(RR_{obs}\)): 0.60
95% Confidence Interval: [0.45, 0.80]

The clinical team is very excited and believes this drug is highly effective. It’s your job to assess how robust this finding is to potential unmeasured confounding.


Task 1: Load Packages
Please load the EValue and tidyverse packages.


Code
# TODO: Fill in the Package Names
if (!require("pacman")) {
  install.packages("pacman")
}
pacman::p_load(..., ...)




Solution: Task 1


# Load the EValue Package for Calculations

# Load Tidyverse for General R Usability
