4 R Code Examples & Interpretation

4.1 Visualizing ITT Vs Per-Protocol Effects


Code
# Create DAG for per-protocol confounding
dag <- dagify(
  Y ~ A + U + Z,
  A ~ Z + U,
  exposure = "A",
  outcome = "Y",
  coords = list(
    x = c(Z = 1, U = 2, A = 3, Y = 4),
    y = c(Z = 2, U = 1, A = 2, Y = 2)
  )
)

# Plot with ggdag
ggdag(dag, text_size = 3.5) +
  theme_dag() +
  labs(
    title = "Per-Protocol Confounding",
    subtitle = "Backdoor path A ← U → Y creates confounding"
  )









Figure 1: Causal diagram showing confounding for per-protocol effect




Interpretation: Even though \(Z\) is randomized (\(Z \perp!!!\perp Y^z\)), the received treatment \(A\) is not randomized relative to \(Y\) due to the common cause \(U\). This necessitates adjustment for \(U\) (or proxies of \(U\)) when estimating per-protocol effects.


4.2 Simulating a Trial with Non-Adherence


Code
set.seed(579)
n <- 1000

# Simulate trial data
trial_data <- tibble(
  id = 1:n,
  # Unmeasured risk factor
  U = rbinom(n, 1, 0.5),
  # Randomized assignment
  Z = rbinom(n, 1, 0.5),
  # Received treatment (adherence depends on U and Z)
  A = case_when(
    Z == 1 ~ 1, # Perfect adherence in treatment arm
    Z == 0 & U == 1 ~ rbinom(n, 1, 0.7), # High-risk seek treatment
    Z == 0 & U == 0 ~ 0, # Low-risk remain untreated
    TRUE ~ 0 # Default case
  ),
  # Outcome (depends on A and U)
  Y = rbinom(
    n,
    1,
    prob = case_when(
      A == 1 & U == 1 ~ 0.20,
      A == 1 & U == 0 ~ 0.10,
      A == 0 & U == 1 ~ 0.60,
      A == 0 & U == 0 ~ 0.30
    )
  )
)

# Calculate effects
trial_summary <- trial_data %>%
  summarise(
    # ITT effect
    ITT_Risk_Z1 = mean(Y[Z == 1]),
    ITT_Risk_Z0 = mean(Y[Z == 0]),
    ITT_RD = ITT_Risk_Z1 - ITT_Risk_Z0,

    # Naive per-protocol (unadjusted)
    PP_Risk_A1 = mean(Y[A == 1]),
    PP_Risk_A0 = mean(Y[A == 0]),
    Naive_PP_RD = PP_Risk_A1 - PP_Risk_A0,

    # True per-protocol (adjusted by U, but U is unmeasured)
    # We can calculate it because we simulated U
    True_PP_RD = 0.5 * (-0.4) + 0.5 * (-0.2)
  )

trial_summary %>%
  pivot_longer(everything(), names_to = "Measure", values_to = "Value") %>%
  gt() %>%
  fmt_number(columns = Value, decimals = 3) %>%
  tab_header(title = "Comparison of ITT and Per-Protocol Estimates")

4.3 Sequential Trial Emulation


Code
# Simulate cohort with multiple eligible times
set.seed(579)
cohort <- expand_grid(
  id = 1:200,
  time = 0:5
) %>%
  group_by(id) %>%
  mutate(
    # Eligibility (e.g., postmenopausal, no chronic disease)
    eligible = time >= rbinom(1, 5, 0.5),
    # Treatment initiation
    initiated = if_else(eligible, rbinom(1, 1, 0.3), 0),
    # Once initiated, stays initiated
    A = cummax(initiated),
    # Outcome risk increases with time and is lower with treatment
    Y = rbinom(1, 1, prob = 0.05 * time - 0.02 * A)
  ) %>%
  ungroup()

# Emulate trials starting at each time point
trial_results <- cohort %>%
  filter(eligible) %>%
  group_by(time) %>%
  nest() %>%
  mutate(
    trial_data = map(
      data,
      ~ {
        # For each time, create trial
        .x %>%
          filter(time == min(time)) %>% # Baseline for this trial
          left_join(
            cohort %>%
              filter(time > min(.x$time)) %>%
              select(id, time, A, Y),
            by = "id"
          )
      }
    ),
    # Estimate effect for each trial
    effect = map_dbl(
      trial_data,
      ~ {
        mean(.x$Y[.x$A == 1], na.rm = TRUE) -
          mean(.x$Y[.x$A == 0], na.rm = TRUE)
      }
    )
  )

# Pool across trials (simple average; proper analysis would use bootstrapping)
trial_results %>%
  summarise(
    n_trials = n(),
    pooled_effect = mean(effect, na.rm = TRUE),
    se_effect = sd(effect, na.rm = TRUE) / sqrt(n())
  ) %>%
  gt() %>%
  fmt_number(decimals = 3) %>%
  tab_header(title = "Pooled Results from Sequential Trial Emulation")

4.4 Cloning for Non-Unique Strategy Assignment


Code
# Simulate individuals whose baseline data are compatible with multiple strategies
set.seed(579)
base_data <- tibble(
  id = 1:100,
  cd4_baseline = rnorm(100, 400, 100)
) %>%
  filter(cd4_baseline > 300 & cd4_baseline < 500) # Eligible for all strategies

# Strategies:
# g1: Initiate immediately
# g2: Initiate when CD4 < 350
# g3: Initiate when CD4 < 200

# Clone each individual into 3 copies
cloned_data <- base_data %>%
  crossing(strategy = c("Immediate", "At_350", "At_200")) %>%
  mutate(clone_id = paste0(id, "_", strategy))

# Simulate follow-up
set.seed(579)
followup <- cloned_data %>%
  crossing(month = 0:12) %>%
  group_by(clone_id) %>%
  mutate(
    # CD4 declines over time (simplified)
    cd4 = cd4_baseline - month * 15 + rnorm(n(), 0, 20),

    # Observed treatment (person's actual behavior, same across clones)
    observed_treatment = case_when(
      month == 0 ~ 0, # Nobody treated at baseline
      month <= 3 ~ 0, # Delay 3 months
      TRUE ~ 1 # Then initiate
    ),

    # Treatment assigned by strategy
    assigned_treatment = case_when(
      strategy == "Immediate" ~ if_else(month >= 0, 1, 0),
      strategy == "At_350" ~ if_else(cd4 < 350, 1, 0),
      strategy == "At_200" ~ if_else(cd4 < 200, 1, 0)
    ),

    # Censor when observed != assigned
    censored = observed_treatment != assigned_treatment,
    censored = cumsum(censored) > 0,

    # Outcome
    death = if_else(
      !censored,
      rbinom(n(), 1, 0.01 + 0.02 * (1 - observed_treatment)),
      NA_integer_
    )
  ) %>%
  ungroup()

# Estimate effect (simplified; would need IP weighting for censoring)
followup %>%
  filter(!censored, month == 12) %>%
  group_by(strategy) %>%
  summarise(
    n = n(),
    deaths = sum(death, na.rm = TRUE),
    risk = mean(death, na.rm = TRUE)
  ) %>%
  gt() %>%
  fmt_number(columns = risk, decimals = 3) %>%
  tab_header(title = "Risk by Strategy (Cloning Approach)")

5 Hands-On R Lab

Lab Objectives

Specify a target trial protocol for a given research question
Identify and classify protocol deviations as adherence vs. non-adherence
Implement sequential trial emulation for multiple eligibility times
Apply cloning for non-unique strategy assignment
Compare ITT and per-protocol analyses



Pre-Lab Reading
Before lab, review:

Hernán & Robins (2020), Chapter 22, Sections 22.1-22.4
The concepts of ITT effect, per-protocol effect, and time zero



Lab Scenario
You have electronic health record data on 5,000 patients with newly diagnosed type 2 diabetes between 2015-2020. You want to estimate the 3-year risk of cardiovascular events under two treatment strategies:

Intensive strategy: Initiate ≥2 medications immediately
Standard strategy: Initiate 1 medication, add others as needed



Task 1: Specify the Target Trial Protocol
Write out the key components of your target trial:


Code
# Target Trial Protocol Specification
# -----------------------------------

# 1. Eligibility criteria:
# Adults (18+) with new type 2 diabetes diagnosis
# No prior diabetes medications
# No cardiovascular disease at diagnosis

# 2. Time zero:
# Date of diabetes diagnosis

# 3. Treatment strategies:
# g1 (intensive): Initiate ≥2 medications within 30 days of diagnosis
# g0 (standard): Initiate 1 medication within 30 days, may add others later

# 4. Outcome:
# Cardiovascular event (MI, stroke, CV death) within 36 months

# 5. Causal contrast:
# Per-protocol effect: Risk difference under full adherence to g1 vs g0

# 6. Analysis plan:
# Sequential trial emulation with monthly time units
# IP weighting for time-varying confounding and censoring




Task 2: Simulate Data and Identify Time Zero


Code
set.seed(20241111)

# Simulate patient cohort
n_patients <- 500 # Reduced for lab

diabetes_cohort <- tibble(
  patient_id = 1:n_patients,

  # Demographics
  age = rnorm(n_patients, 55, 10),
  female = rbinom(n_patients, 1, 0.45),

  # Diagnosis date (time zero!)
  dx_date = as.Date("2015-01-01") + runif(n_patients, 0, 365 * 5),

  # Baseline risk factors
  hba1c_baseline = rnorm(n_patients, 8.5, 1.5),
  sbp_baseline = rnorm(n_patients, 140, 20),

  # Treatment initiation
  days_to_treat = rexp(n_patients, 1 / 60) * (1 + 0.5 * (hba1c_baseline > 9)),

  # Number of initial medications (strategy assignment)
  n_meds_initial = case_when(
    days_to_treat <= 30 & hba1c_baseline > 9 ~ rpois(n_patients, 2),
    days_to_treat <= 30 ~ 1,
    TRUE ~ 0
  )
) %>%
  mutate(
    strategy = case_when(
      n_meds_initial >= 2 ~ "Intensive",
      n_meds_initial == 1 ~ "Standard",
      TRUE ~ "None"
    )
  )

# Inspect time zero
diabetes_cohort %>%
  select(patient_id, dx_date, days_to_treat, n_meds_initial, strategy) %>%
  head(10) %>%
  gt() %>%

text:
Check Your Understanding
Q1: Why is dx_date the correct time zero? A1: It’s when eligibility criteria are met (new diabetes diagnosis, no prior meds), and when treatment strategies would be assigned in the target trial.
Q2: What would be wrong with using days_to_treat as time zero? A2: This varies across patients and occurs after diagnosis. Starting follow-up at treatment initiation would: - Exclude patients who died before treatment - Miss early treatment effects - Create selection bias if sicker patients delay treatment

title: Week 13: Target Trial Emulation
text:
Quick Knowledge Check
Q1: True or False: The ITT effect from a randomized trial always requires no adjustment for confounding. A1: False. While baseline confounding is eliminated by randomization, loss to follow-up can create post-randomization selection bias requiring adjustment.
Q2: What makes a conventional “per-protocol analysis” (restricting to adherers) potentially biased? A2: Adherence is post-randomization and typically related to prognosis, creating confounding through \(A \leftarrow U \rightarrow Y\). Simply restricting to adherers doesn’t eliminate this bias.
Q3: Why might a per-protocol analysis be more informative than ITT for decision-making? A3: Decision-makers typically want to know the effect of actually following a treatment strategy, not the effect of being assigned to it with uncertain adherence patterns.

title: Week 13: Target Trial Emulation
text:
6 Common Pitfalls & Checks






WarningPitfall 1: Misunderstanding “Per-Protocol”



Wrong: “Per-protocol analysis just means restricting to people who adhered.” Right: Per-protocol effect is a causal contrast requiring adjustment for confounding, just like any observational analysis.
Check: Did you adjust for factors predicting adherence and outcome? If not, your estimate is biased.








WarningPitfall 2: Immortal Time Bias



Wrong: Starting follow-up at treatment initiation for the treated group but at an earlier time for controls. Right: All groups must have the same time zero—when eligibility is met and strategies could be assigned.
Check: Can every individual die/experience the outcome at any time after time zero? If treatment group has “immortal time” before treatment, you have bias.








WarningPitfall 3: Censoring Medically-Indicated Treatment Changes



Wrong: Censoring anyone who stops treatment, including those who stop due to toxicity. Right: Realistic strategies include rules like “stop if toxicity occurs.” Following this rule is adherence, not deviation.
Check: Does your protocol explicitly define when treatment changes are mandated? If stopping for toxicity is required, don’t censor those patients.








WarningPitfall 4: Assuming ITT Is Always Conservative



Wrong: “The ITT effect is always closer to the null than the true effect, so it’s safe.” Right: In head-to-head trials or with high non-adherence, ITT can be further from the null than the per-protocol effect.
Check: Don’t rely on ITT being conservative for safety assessment. Estimate per-protocol effects when evaluating harms.








WarningPitfall 5: Ignoring Time-Varying Confounding



Wrong: Using standard regression to adjust for baseline covariates when treatments and confounders vary over time. Right: Use g-methods (IP weighting, g-formula, g-estimation) when \(A_{k-1} \rightarrow L_k \rightarrow A_k\).
Check: Draw a DAG. If past treatment affects future confounders, standard regression fails. Use g-methods.








ImportantEssential Pre-Analysis Checks



Before analyzing any comparative study:

Write out the target trial protocol - What would the RCT look like?
Define time zero precisely - When is eligibility met?
Specify treatment strategies exactly - What actions at what times?
Distinguish adherence from deviation - What changes are mandated by the protocol?
Identify time-varying confounders - What post-baseline factors affect both treatment and outcome?
Choose appropriate methods - Do you need g-methods or will standard methods suffice?

text:
7 Advanced Teaching Activities & Interactivity

7.1 Flipped Classroom: Protocol Critique
Pre-Class: Students read a published observational study and identify the implicit target trial.
In-Class: Small groups critique the study:

What was the time zero?
What strategies were compared?
Were there time-zero errors?
What confounders were adjusted for?
Were g-methods needed?

Present findings to class and discuss.


7.2 Think-Pair-Share: When Is ITT Sufficient?
Prompt: “Your collaborator says: ‘Randomization eliminates confounding, so we just need an ITT analysis. Why complicate things with per-protocol?’ How do you respond?”
Think (2 min): Write down your response Pair (3 min): Discuss with a partner Share (10 min): Class discussion
Teaching Points:

Randomization eliminates baseline confounding for effect of assignment
Doesn’t eliminate post-randomization selection bias (LTFU)
Doesn’t eliminate confounding for per-protocol effect
ITT may not answer the policy question



7.3 Case Study: Hormone Therapy Controversy
Present the Women’s Health Initiative randomized trial vs. observational studies of postmenopausal hormone therapy:

Observational: Protective effect on CHD
WHI Trial: Harmful effect on CHD

Group Activity: Analyze why estimates differed. Consider:

Different populations (healthy user bias)
Different time zeros (initiation at menopause vs. years later)
Different durations of follow-up
Different outcome ascertainment

Key Learning: Many “trial vs. observational study” discrepancies reflect poor emulation rather than fundamental limitations of observational data.


7.4 Interactive Simulation: Explore Non-Adherence Patterns
Provide R Shiny app where students manipulate:

Degree of non-adherence (0-100%)
Direction of confounding (high-risk more vs. less likely to adhere)
Strength of treatment effect

Observe effects on:

ITT estimate
Naive per-protocol estimate
Adjusted per-protocol estimate

Discussion: When does ITT fail to be conservative? When is adjustment most critical?


7.5 Retrieval Practice: Spaced Quizzing
Week 1: Define ITT and per-protocol effects Week 3: Identify time-zero errors in example studies Week 5: Determine when g-methods are needed Week 7: Design a target trial emulation
Each quiz includes:

Multiple-choice questions

Code-reading exercises (identify errors in provided R code)

Question 1: In a randomized trial with sustained treatment strategies, which statement is TRUE?
A. ITT analysis never requires adjustment for any variables B. Per-protocol analysis only requires adjustment for baseline confounders C. Both ITT and per-protocol analyses may require g-methods for time-varying factors D. Only observational studies need adjustment for time-varying confounding
Correct: C

Students vote individually (30 sec)

Vote again
Instructor explains correct answer

title: Week 13: Target Trial Emulation
text:
8 Appendix: Advanced Theory & Derivations

8.1 Formal Definition of Per-Protocol Effect Under Sustained Strategies
Let \(\bar{A}_k = (A_0, A_1, \ldots, A_k)\) denote treatment history through time \(k\). A treatment strategy \(g\) is a function that assigns treatment \(A_k\) at time \(k\) based on past information:
\[
g: (\bar{A}_{k-1}, \bar{L}_k) \mapsto \{0, 1\}
\]
where \(\bar{L}_k\) is covariate history through \(k\). The strategy \(g\) can be:

Static: \(g(\bar{A}_{k-1}, \bar{L}_k) = a\) for all \(k\) (always treat or never treat)
Dynamic: \(g(\bar{A}_{k-1}, \bar{L}_k)\) depends on \(\bar{L}_k\) (e.g., “treat if CD4 < 200”)

Per-Protocol Effect: For strategies \(g\) and \(g'\), the per-protocol effect at time \(K\) is:
\[
\Delta_{PP} = E[Y_K^g] - E[Y_K^{g'}]
\]
where \(Y_K^g\) is the outcome at time \(K\) under strategy \(g\).

Identification Conditions
To identify \(E[Y_K^g]\) from observed data, we require:

Consistency: \(Y_K = Y_K^{\bar{a}}\) when \(\bar{A} = \bar{a}\)
Sequential exchangeability: \(Y_K^{\bar{a}} \perp!!!\perp A_k \mid \bar{A}_{k-1}, \bar{L}_k\) for all \(k\)
Positivity: \(\Pr[A_k = g(\bar{A}_{k-1}, \bar{L}_k) \mid \bar{A}_{k-1}, \bar{L}_k] > 0\) for all \(k\)

Under these conditions:
\[
E[Y_K^g] = \int E[Y_K \mid \bar{A} = \bar{a}^g, \bar{L}] \prod_{k=0}^{K-1} f(L_k \mid \bar{A}_{k-1}, \bar{L}_{k-1}) d\bar{L}
\]
where \(\bar{a}^g\) is the treatment path assigned by strategy \(g\).
Proof Sketch: By sequential exchangeability and consistency, we can express the counterfactual mean as an iterated expectation over observed data distributions.



8.2 When Does ITT Equal Per-Protocol Effect?
Theorem: The ITT effect equals the per-protocol effect if and only if:

Perfect adherence: \(A_k = g_z(k)\) for all \(k\), where \(g_z\) is the strategy assigned by \(Z\)
Exclusion restriction: \(Z\) affects \(Y\) only through \(\bar{A}\)

Proof:
Under perfect adherence and exclusion restriction:
\[
E[Y_K^{z=1}] = E[Y_K^{g_1}]
\]
\[
E[Y_K^{z=0}] = E[Y_K^{g_0}]
\]
Therefore:
\[
\Delta_{ITT} = E[Y_K^{z=1}] - E[Y_K^{z=0}] = E[Y_K^{g_1}] - E[Y_K^{g_0}] = \Delta_{PP}
\]
Numeric Example:
Consider a 2-period trial (\(k \in \{0,1\}\), outcome at \(k=2\)):

Perfect adherence: All \(Z=1\) follow \(g_1\): \((A_0=1, A_1=1)\); all \(Z=0\) follow \(g_0\): \((A_0=0, A_1=0)\)
Exclusion restriction holds

Suppose true counterfactual risks:
\[
\Pr[Y_2^{g_1}=1] = 0.20
\]
\[
\Pr[Y_2^{g_0}=1] = 0.30
\]
Then observed risks:
\[
\Pr[Y_2=1|Z=1] = \Pr[Y_2^{g_1}=1] = 0.20
\]
\[
\Pr[Y_2=1|Z=0] = \Pr[Y_2^{g_0}=1] = 0.30
\]
Thus \(\Delta_{ITT} = \Delta_{PP} = -0.10\).


8.3 Selection Bias from Loss to Follow-Up in ITT Analysis
Even with randomization, censoring \(C\) can induce selection bias for the ITT effect.
DAG:
\[
Z \rightarrow A \rightarrow L \rightarrow C
\]
\[
L \rightarrow Y
\]
Conditioning on \(C=0\) opens collider-stratification bias via \(Z \rightarrow A \rightarrow L \leftarrow C\).
Formal Proof:
We want \(E[Y^{z=1,c=0}] - E[Y^{z=0,c=0}]\), but observe:
\[
E[Y \mid Z=1, C=0] - E[Y \mid Z=0, C=0]
\]
These differ because:
\[
E[Y \mid Z=z, C=0] = \sum_\ell E[Y \mid Z=z, C=0, L=\ell] \Pr[L=\ell \mid Z=z, C=0]
\]
The distribution \(\Pr[L \mid Z=z, C=0]\) differs from \(\Pr[L^z]\) due to selection on \(C\).
IP Weighting Solution:
Create weights:
\[
W = \frac{1}{\Pr[C=0 \mid Z, L]}
\]
Then:
\[
E\left[\frac{Y \cdot I(C=0)}{\Pr[C=0 \mid Z, L]} \mid Z=z\right] = E[Y^{z,c=0}]
\]
Numeric Example:



Group
\(\Pr[Y=1 \mid C=0]\)
\(\Pr[C=0]\)
True \(E[Y^{z,c=0}]\)




\(Z=1\)

\(Z=0\)

Naive estimate (complete cases): \(0.15 - 0.25 = -0.10\) True ITT effect: \(0.18 - 0.24 = -0.06\) Bias: \(-0.04\) (underestimates benefit)
With IP weighting:
\[
W_{Z=1} = \frac{1}{0.90}, \quad W_{Z=0} = \frac{1}{0.95}
\]
Weighted estimate recovers \(-0.06\).


8.4 Cloning + Censoring + Weighting: Formal Justification
Setup: At baseline, individual \(i\)’s data are consistent with strategies \(\{g_1, g_2, \ldots, g_m\}\). We cannot uniquely assign them to one strategy.
Procedure:

Create \(m\) clones \(\{i_1, i_2, \ldots, i_m\}\), assign each to one strategy
At each time \(k\), censor clone \(i_j\) if observed treatment \(A_k\) violates strategy \(g_j\)
Weight by inverse probability of remaining uncensored

Key Result: If censoring at time \(k\) depends on \((\bar{A}_{k-1}, \bar{L}_k)\), and we weight by:
\[
W_k = \prod_{j=0}^{k-1} \frac{1}{\Pr[C_{j+1}=0 \mid \bar{A}_j, \bar{L}_j, C_j=0]}
\]
Then:
\[
E\left[\frac{Y_K \cdot I(\bar{C}=\bar{0})}{\prod_k W_k} \mid g\right] = E[Y_K^g]
\]
Proof Sketch: By sequential exchangeability of censoring:
\[
E[Y_K^{g,\bar{c}=\bar{0}}] = E\left[E[Y_K \mid \bar{A}=\bar{a}^g, \bar{C}=\bar{0}, \bar{L}] \prod_k \Pr[C_{k+1}=0 \mid \bar{A}_k, \bar{L}_k]\right]
\]
The weight \(1/\Pr[C_{k+1}=0 \mid \cdots]\) removes the selection.
Numeric Example:
Two strategies: \(g_1\) (immediate treatment), \(g_2\) (delay treatment).
Person 1 delays treatment:

Clone 1 (assigned \(g_1\)): Censored at \(k=0\) when treatment not initiated

Weight at censoring: \(W_0 = 1/\Pr[\text{initiate} \mid L_0] = 1/0.30 = 3.33\)

Clone 2 (assigned \(g_2\)): Remains uncensored

If dies at \(k=5\): Contributes death to \(g_2\) strategy
Weight: \(W_5 = \prod_{k=0}^4 1/\Pr[C_{k+1}=0 \mid \bar{A}_k, \bar{L}_k]\)


Person 2 initiates immediately, then stops at \(k=2\) due to toxicity (mandated by \(g_1\)):

Clone 1 (assigned \(g_1\)): Remains uncensored (stopping is adherence)
Clone 2 (assigned \(g_2\)): Censored at \(k=0\) when treatment initiated



8.5 Bias Decomposition for Naive Per-Protocol Analysis
Setting: Randomized trial with non-adherence. True per-protocol effect \(\Delta_{PP}\), observed naive estimate \(\hat{\Delta}_{\text{naive}}\) comparing \(A=1\) vs \(A=0\) without adjustment.
Bias:
\[
\text{Bias} = E[\hat{\Delta}_{\text{naive}}] - \Delta_{PP}
\]
Can be decomposed:
\[
\text{Bias} = \underbrace{\text{Confounding bias}}_{\text{Selection into } A} + \underbrace{\text{Selection bias}}_{\text{Censoring/LTFU}}
\]
Confounding bias:
\[
E[Y \mid A=1] - E[Y \mid A=0] = \underbrace{E[Y^{a=1}] - E[Y^{a=0}]}_{\text{Causal effect}} + \underbrace{E[Y^{a=0} \mid A=1] - E[Y^{a=0} \mid A=0]}_{\text{Confounding}}
\]
Selection bias (if conditioning on \(C=0\)):
\[
E[Y \mid A=a, C=0] \neq E[Y^{a,c=0}]
\]
Numeric Example:
Suppose unmeasured \(U\) (high-risk):










\(U\)
\(\Pr[U]\)
\(\Pr[A=1 \mid U]\)
\(E[Y^{a=1} \mid U]\)
\(E[Y^{a=0} \mid U]\)

True PP effect:
\[
\Delta_{PP} = 0.5(-0.40) + 0.5(-0.20) = -0.30
\]
Naive estimate:
\[
\Pr[A=1] = 0.5(0.7) + 0.5(0.3) = 0.50
\]
\[
E[Y \mid A=1] = \frac{0.5(0.7)(0.20) + 0.5(0.3)(0.10)}{0.50} = 0.155
\]
\[
E[Y \mid A=0] = \frac{0.5(0.3)(0.60) + 0.5(0.7)(0.30)}{0.50} = 0.285

\[
E[Y^{a=0} \mid A=1] - E[Y^{a=0} \mid A=0] = 0.515 - 0.315 = +0.20
\]
This positive confounding (high-risk more likely treated) attenuates the beneficial effect.

title: Week 13: Target Trial Emulation
text:
Welcome to our final substantive week of the course. Over the past eleven weeks, we have amassed a powerful toolkit for causal inference: DAGs, potential outcomes, confounding control, propensity scores, instrumental variables, and methods for time-varying exposures. We have treated these as distinct topics, each with its own set of assumptions and procedures.
This week, we synthesize everything we have learned into a single, cohesive framework: Target Trial Emulation. This framework, powerfully articulated by Hernán & Robins (2020), provides a structured approach to designing and critiquing observational causal inference studies. The core idea is that every causal question can and should be framed as an attempt to emulate a hypothetical, perfectly-designed (but often infeasible) randomized controlled trial—the “target trial.”
By explicitly specifying the protocol of this ideal target trial, we can then systematically evaluate how our observational analysis succeeds or fails in emulating it. This process makes our assumptions transparent, our design choices deliberate, and our limitations clear. It moves us from a scattered application of statistical methods to a principled, trial-centric approach to causal inference. This week is not about learning a new statistical method, but about learning a new way to think.

title: Week 13: Target Trial Emulation
text:
1. Comprehensive Topic Explanation

The Unifying Idea: Observational Studies as Attempts to Emulate a Trial
The central premise of the target trial framework is that for any causal question, there is an ideal (though perhaps hypothetical) randomized experiment that could answer it. This ideal experiment is the target trial. When we conduct an observational study, what we are really trying to do is use observational data and sophisticated analytical methods to emulate that target trial as closely as possible.
Why is this framework so powerful?

It provides a common language: Trialists, epidemiologists, and data scientists can all understand the components of a trial protocol.
It forces clarity: Vague causal questions like “What is the effect of statins?” must be refined into specific, answerable questions by defining the components of the trial.
It illuminates sources of bias: Biases in observational studies can be elegantly reframed as specific deviations from the target trial’s protocol.



The Seven Components of a Target Trial Protocol
To emulate a trial, we must first explicitly design it. A trial protocol consists of seven key components. For each component, we must consider its ideal form and its observational analogue.

Eligibility Criteria:

Target Trial: Who would be included in the trial? This involves defining the study population based on factors like age, disease status, and prior medical history. Crucially, eligibility must be determined before treatment assignment.
Observational Analogue: This corresponds to the inclusion/exclusion criteria for our observational cohort. A common mistake is to select individuals based on information recorded after their treatment has already started, which can introduce selection bias.

Treatment Strategies:

Target Trial: What, exactly, are the interventions being compared? A “treatment strategy” is a rule that specifies the intervention over time. It must be well-defined and realistic. “Take statins” is vague. “Initiate 40mg of atorvastatin daily at baseline and continue unless a severe side effect occurs” is a well-defined strategy.
Observational Analogue: We must identify groups in our data that appear to follow the specified strategies. This can be challenging. For example, in the real world, people’s adherence to a medication plan is not perfect.

Assignment Procedure:

Target Trial: How are individuals assigned to a treatment strategy? In an ideal trial, this is random assignment. Randomization is the key to ensuring that, on average, the treatment groups are exchangeable at baseline.
Observational Analogue: This is the most critical point of departure. In observational studies, assignment is not random. People’s doctors and they themselves choose treatments based on prognostic factors. This is the origin of confounding. Our causal inference methods (propensity scores, standardization, IV) are all attempts to adjust for the lack of randomization.

Follow-up Period:

Target Trial: When does follow-up begin and end for each individual? Follow-up must begin at the moment of randomization (Time Zero).
Observational Analogue: We must define a “Time Zero” in our observational data that corresponds to the start of the treatment strategy. Forgetting to do this is a common source of “immortal time bias,” where, for example, a person must survive for a period of time before they can be classified as “treated,” leading to a spurious protective effect.

Outcome:

Target Trial: What is the outcome of interest, and how and when is it measured? (e.g., incidence of myocardial infarction within 5 years).
Observational Analogue: The outcome definition should be identical. We must ensure it is ascertained equally in all treatment groups to avoid detection bias.

Causal Contrast (Estimand):

Target Trial: What is the specific causal question? Are we interested in the Intention-to-Treat (ITT) effect (the effect of being assigned to a strategy, regardless of adherence) or the Per-Protocol effect (the effect of actually adhering to the strategy)?
Observational Analogue: This choice has major implications for our analysis. Emulating an ITT effect is often more straightforward (comparing groups based on initial treatment), while emulating a per-protocol effect requires methods like MSMs to handle time-varying confounding and adherence.

Analysis Plan:

Target Trial: How will the causal contrast be estimated? In a simple trial, this might be a comparison of risks or means.
Observational Analogue: This is where our entire toolkit comes into play. The analysis plan specifies the method chosen to adjust for the lack of randomization—be it IPTW to handle time-varying confounding for a per-protocol analysis, or a baseline propensity score model to emulate a simple ITT analysis.

title: Week 13: Target Trial Emulation
text:
2. Intuitive Clarifications of Challenging Ideas

Analogy: The “Coffee and Heart Disease” Study
Imagine we want to answer the question: “Does drinking coffee cause heart disease?” This is a vague question. Let’s use the target trial framework to make it concrete.
Designing the Target Trial:

Eligibility: We might enroll adults aged 40-65 with no prior history of heart disease.
Treatment Strategies: We’ll compare two strategies: (1) “Abstain from all caffeinated coffee for 10 years” vs. (2) “Drink 2 cups of caffeinated coffee every morning for 10 years.”
Assignment: We would randomly assign eligible participants to one of the two strategies.
Follow-up: We would start follow-up at the moment of randomization and continue for 10 years.
Outcome: The outcome is the incidence of a major cardiovascular event (e.g., heart attack, stroke).
Causal Contrast: We might be interested in the per-protocol effect—the effect among those who actually stuck to their assigned coffee-drinking (or abstaining) plan.
Analysis Plan: Compare the 10-year risk of cardiovascular events between the two groups.

Emulating the Trial with Observational Data: Now, we take our observational dataset (e.g., the NHANES survey) and try to emulate this trial.

Eligibility: We select people in our data who meet the eligibility criteria at the start of our observation period.
Treatment Strategies: We find people in the data whose reported coffee intake roughly matches our two strategies.
Assignment: This is the problem. In the real world, people who drink coffee are different from those who don’t (they might smoke more, exercise less, etc.). This is confounding.
Analysis Plan to Fix Assignment: Our analysis plan must now include a method to adjust for these differences. Since behaviors like smoking can change over time and influence future coffee drinking, we likely have time-varying confounding. Therefore, our analysis plan would specify using a Marginal Structural Model with IPTW to estimate the per-protocol effect we desire.

By structuring our thinking this way, we see that the choice of using an MSM was not arbitrary; it was dictated by the specific causal question (per-protocol effect) and the specific challenges (time-varying confounding) that arose from emulating our target trial.


Intention-to-Treat vs. Per-Protocol: A Key Distinction








Causal Question
Intention-to-Treat (ITT) Effect
Per-Protocol Effect




What it answers
What is the effect of prescribing or assigning a treatment strategy?
What is the effect of adhering to a treatment strategy?


Analogy to Trial
Compares groups based on their randomized assignment, regardless of what they actually did (“as randomized”).
Compares groups based on what treatment they actually received and adhered to.


Bias in an Ideal Trial
Unbiased for the effect of assignment. Preserves the benefits of randomization.
Can be biased even in a trial, as adherence is a post-randomization behavior.


Observational Emulation
Simpler. Requires adjusting for baseline confounders only. Example: Propensity score matching on initial treatment.
More complex. Requires adjusting for baseline and time-varying confounders that affect adherence. Example: MSMs.


Usefulness
Pragmatic. Useful for policy makers deciding whether to recommend a strategy.
Explanatory. Useful for scientists understanding the biological effects of a treatment if taken as intended.

title: Week 13: Target Trial Emulation
text:
3. Simple, Hand-Calculation Numerical Example(s)
Since this week is conceptual, we won’t do a numerical calculation of an effect. Instead, our “by-hand” example will be to design a target trial protocol on paper.
Causal Question: Does starting a vegan diet cause weight change in overweight adults?
Step-by-Step Protocol Design:

Eligibility Criteria:

Include adults aged 18-65.
Include individuals with a Body Mass Index (BMI) between 25 and 35 kg/m².
Exclude individuals who are already vegetarian or vegan.
Exclude pregnant individuals.
Exclude individuals with medical conditions that would contraindicate a vegan diet.

Treatment Strategies:

Strategy 1 (Intervention): Follow a vegan diet for 12 months. A vegan diet is defined as excluding all meat, poultry, fish, dairy, eggs, and honey.
Strategy 2 (Control): Continue with your usual diet for 12 months.

Assignment Procedure:

Target Trial: Randomly assign eligible participants 1:1 to either Strategy 1 or Strategy 2.

Follow-up Period:

Follow-up begins at the time of randomization (Day 0).
Follow-up ends after 12 months.

Outcome:

The primary outcome is the change in body weight (in kg) from baseline to 12 months.

Causal Contrast (Estimand):

We are interested in the Intention-to-Treat effect: the effect of being assigned to the vegan diet strategy, regardless of how well participants adhered to it. This answers the pragmatic question, “What is the effect of recommending a vegan diet?”

Analysis Plan:

Target Trial: At 12 months, calculate the mean weight change in the group assigned to the vegan diet and the mean weight change in the group assigned to the usual diet. The ATE is the difference between these two means.
Observational Emulation: If we were using observational data, our analysis plan would need to adjust for baseline confounders (e.g., age, sex, baseline activity level) that differ between people who spontaneously adopt a vegan diet and those who don’t. We could use propensity score matching or g-computation on the baseline covariates.


This simple exercise transforms a vague question into a precise, answerable scientific query.

title: Week 13: Target Trial Emulation
text:
4. R Code Examples & Interpretation
The key challenge in observational studies is the non-random assignment. We can visualize this difference with ggdag.

The Ideal Trial vs. The Observational Reality

Code
# In an ideal trial, assignment (A) is random, so it has no parents.
trial_dag <- dagify(
    Y ~ A,
    exposure = "A",
    outcome = "Y"
)
ggdag(trial_dag) + labs(title = "Ideal Randomized Trial")

# In an observational study, confounders (L) affect both assignment (A) and outcome (Y).
obs_dag <- dagify(
    Y ~ A + L,
    A ~ L,
    exposure = "A",
    outcome = "Y"
)
ggdag(obs_dag) + labs(title = "Observational Reality")












(a) Ideal Randomized Trial











(b) Observational Reality with Confounding







Figure 1: Causal DAGs for a Randomized Trial vs. an Observational Study



Interpretation:

Ideal Trial DAG: The beauty of a randomized trial is its simplicity. There are no arrows pointing into the exposure A. This means there are no backdoor paths between A and the outcome Y. The association between A and Y is the causal effect.
Observational DAG: This is the world we usually live in. There is a confounder L that is a common cause of both A and Y, creating a backdoor path (A <- L -> Y). If we naively calculate the association between A and Y, we get a mix of the true causal effect and spurious association from this open backdoor.

The target trial framework tells us that the goal of our observational analysis plan is to find a way to make the observational DAG behave like the trial DAG. Methods like propensity score weighting or g-computation are tools designed to close that backdoor path, allowing us to isolate the true causal arrow A -> Y.

title: Week 13: Target Trial Emulation
text:
5. Hands-On R Lab

Lab: Designing a Target Trial for Your Final Project
Purpose: This lab is a capstone workshop. It is designed to help you synthesize the concepts from the course and apply them to your own research question using the structured thinking of the target trial framework.
Lab Objectives:

Take a real-world causal question and formalize it by specifying the seven components of a target trial protocol.
Identify the key points where an observational study attempting to answer this question would deviate from the ideal trial.
Choose an appropriate analytical method from this course to address those deviations.

Instructions: For this lab, you will not be writing R code to analyze data. You will be writing a research protocol in a Quarto document. Choose a causal question you are interested in (this could be for your final project or another topic of interest). Create a new Quarto document and, using the seven components below as your section headers, write out the protocol for the ideal target trial that would answer your question.
Then, for each section, add a subsection called “Observational Emulation Challenges” where you describe the specific problems you would face trying to implement this part of the protocol using real-world observational data.

Example Project: Effect of Statin Therapy on Heart Disease
Here is a filled-out example to guide you.
1. Eligibility Criteria

Target Trial Protocol: We will enroll individuals aged 40-75 who have not had a prior cardiovascular event but have at least one risk factor (e.g., hypertension, high cholesterol).
Observational Emulation Challenges: In our electronic health record data, we must be careful to define eligibility based only on information available before the first statin prescription (or a corresponding index date for non-users). If we include people who had a heart attack before starting statins, we will have selection bias.

2. Treatment Strategies

Target Trial Protocol: We will compare two strategies: (1) “Initiate a moderate-intensity statin (e.g., atorvastatin 20mg) at baseline” vs. (2) “No statin therapy.”
Observational Emulation Challenges: In the real world, people may not adhere to their prescription, or they may switch doses or types of statins. We must decide if we are emulating an “intention-to-treat” effect (based on first prescription) or a “per-protocol” effect, which would require tracking adherence over time.

3. Assignment Procedure

Target Trial Protocol: Randomly assign eligible participants to one of the two strategies.
Observational Emulation Challenges: This is the main deviation. In our data, doctors prescribe statins to patients they believe are at higher risk. This is confounding by indication. The groups are not exchangeable at baseline.

4. Follow-up Period

Target Trial Protocol: Follow-up begins at randomization and continues for 5 years.
Observational Emulation Challenges: We must define Time Zero carefully. For treated individuals, it’s the date of their first prescription. For untreated individuals, we must assign a comparable index date. If we don’t, we can introduce immortal time bias. We also have to worry about loss to follow-up (censoring).

5. Outcome

Target Trial Protocol: The primary outcome is the first occurrence of a major adverse cardiovascular event (MACE).
Observational Emulation Challenges: We must ensure that MACE is recorded with equal accuracy for both statin users and non-users. If statin users have more frequent doctor visits, events might be detected more often, leading to ascertainment bias.

6. Causal Contrast

Target Trial Protocol: We will estimate the Intention-to-Treat effect.
Observational Emulation Challenges: Emulating the ITT effect is feasible. We will compare the group that received an initial statin prescription to the group that did not.

7. Analysis Plan

Target Trial Protocol: Compare the 5-year risk of MACE between the two randomized groups.
Observational Emulation Challenges: To address the confounding from the non-random assignment, our analysis plan must include an adjustment method. To estimate the ITT effect, we can use propensity score matching based on a rich set of baseline covariates (age, sex, comorbidities, baseline cholesterol, etc.) measured at Time Zero. The goal is to create two groups that, at baseline, have a similar probability of having been prescribed a statin, thus emulating randomization.

title: Week 13: Target Trial Emulation
text:
6. Common Pitfalls & Checks






WarningImmortal Time Bias



A frequent and subtle error in emulating trials is the incorrect handling of time. “Immortal time” is a period of follow-up during which, by design, the outcome of interest cannot occur. For example, if you define your “treated” group as “patients who took a drug for at least 6 months,” then by definition, everyone in your treated group had to survive for at least 6 months to be included. This creates a spurious survival advantage for the treated group. The solution is to always start follow-up at a consistently defined Time Zero for everyone, before treatment has begun.








ImportantSpecificity is Your Best Defense Against Bias



The target trial framework’s greatest strength is that it forces you to be relentlessly specific. Vague terms like “effect,” “exposure,” and “outcome” are not allowed. You must define the precise strategies, population, and timeline. This specificity is what allows you to clearly see the potential mismatches between the ideal trial and your observational data, which are the sources of bias.

title: Week 13: Target Trial Emulation
text:
7. Advanced Teaching Activities & Interactivity

“Critique the Paper” Exercise:

Activity: I will provide the abstract and methods section of a published observational study. In small groups, your task will be to reverse-engineer the target trial that the authors were implicitly trying to emulate.
Task: Write down the 7 protocol components for their target trial. Then, identify the most significant deviation in the authors’ observational study and discuss whether their chosen analysis plan (e.g., a simple multivariable regression) was sufficient to address it.

Think-Pair-Share: The “Pragmatic” Trial:

Think: “Many modern RCTs are ‘pragmatic trials,’ where treatment assignment is random, but adherence and follow-up are left to be as they would in the real world. How does this blur the line between a trial and an observational study? Which biases that we’ve discussed for observational studies might still be present in a pragmatic trial, especially when estimating a per-protocol effect?”
Pair: Discuss with a neighbor. Key points might include confounding by indication when analyzing adherence.
Share: We’ll discuss how the target trial framework helps us understand that even some RCTs are not “perfect,” and the same causal principles apply.

title: Overall Project Guidelines
text:
Purpose
The final project is designed to integrate conceptual, methodological, and applied skills in causal inference. Students will pose and answer a causal question using real or simulated data, grounding their analysis in the target trial emulation framework.
The project should demonstrate:

Clear articulation of a STAT 579 Final Project Guidelinesusal estimand (not just a statistical parameter).
Careful identification strategy with explicit assumptions.
Implementation of at least one modern estimation method (e.g., IPW, matching, IV, MSM).
Critical sensitivity checks and interpretation within a real-world context.

title: Overall Project Guidelines
text:
Timeline & Deliverables

Week 1–2: Causal Question Definition

Submit a 1–2 paragraph causal question relevant to biostatistics, epidemiology, or social/biomedical sciences.
Include justification of why the question is causal (not associational).

Week 3–4: Preliminary DAG

Provide a directed acyclic graph (using dagitty or ggdag).
State which paths must be blocked for identification.
Identify potential sources of bias (confounding, selection, measurement error).

Week 5–6: Identification Strategy

Explicitly state whether exchangeability, positivity, SUTVA, and consistency are plausible.
Describe your strategy: backdoor adjustment, IV, MSM, or mediation.

Week 9: Project Proposal (10% of course grade)

3–5 pages.
Elements:

Research question & target trial specification (eligibility, treatment strategies, follow-up, outcome).
DAG & assumptions.
Identification strategy.
Planned data source (public dataset, your own research, or simulation).
Anticipated challenges.


Weeks 10–13: Analysis

Implement at least one causal method (e.g., IPW, g-computation, IV, mediation, MSM).
Provide R code and output with clear interpretation.
Conduct diagnostics (balance checks, overlap, weak instrument tests, model fit).
Perform at least one sensitivity analysis (e.g., E-values, Rosenbaum bounds, tipr).

Week 14: Presentation (10%)

12–15 minutes, conference-style.
Emphasize assumptions, robustness, and substantive conclusions—not just technical detail.

Final Paper (25%) – Due Finals Week

~12–15 pages, structured as a research article:

Introduction: Causal question and motivation.
Target Trial Protocol: Eligibility, treatment, follow-up, outcome, causal estimand.
Assumptions & Identification: DAG, assumptions, strategy.
Methods: Data source, causal methods used, software.
Results: Estimates, sensitivity analyses, robustness checks.
Discussion: Interpretation, limitations, implications.
Appendix: R code (clean, annotated).

title: Overall Project Guidelines
text:
Detailed Instructions

Step 1: Choosing a Question

Prefer health, social, or biomedical contexts (e.g., effect of smoking on lung cancer, impact of job training on income, role of diet on heart disease).
The question must be causal, not descriptive.

Bad: “What factors are associated with depression?”
Good: “What is the effect of exercise on reducing depression severity?”




Step 2: DAG Construction

Must use dagitty or ggdag.
Include confounders, colliders, mediators, and selection mechanisms.
Explicitly identify adjustment set(s) and whether positivity holds.



Step 3: Identification & Assumptions

Address the three pillars:

Exchangeability (unconfoundedness, or IV/exclusion restriction justification).
Positivity (overlap diagnostics, trimming if needed).
Consistency & SUTVA (intervention is well-defined).




Step 4: Method Implementation

Choose a method appropriate to your design:

Backdoor adjustment: matching, stratification, regression, IPW.
IV: LATE, 2SLS.
Mediation: NDE/NIE decomposition.
MSM: time-varying exposures.

Use R packages: MatchIt, WeightIt, ivreg, mediation, EValue, tipr.



Step 5: Sensitivity Analysis

Required to evaluate robustness. Options:

E-value.
Rosenbaum bounds.
Simulated confounding (tipr).




Step 6: Writing & Presentation

Clarity of assumptions is more important than fancy methods.
Discussion must explicitly state: “If assumption X fails, my estimate is biased because…”

title: STAT 579: Final Paper Grading Rubric
text:
This rubric outlines the criteria for evaluating your final project paper. The paper is graded out of 100 points and accounts for 25% of your final course grade. Each component will be assessed on its clarity, rigor, and thoughtful application of causal inference principles.










Component
Weight
Criteria for Excellence (A)
Criteria for Proficiency (B)
Criteria for Developing (C/Below)




Intro & Background
10 pts
Causal question is precise and well-motivated with relevant literature. A clear gap in knowledge is established.
Causal question is clear. Motivation is adequate but may lack depth or context.
Causal question is vague or associational. Motivation is unclear or missing.


Methods: Target Trial Protocol
20 pts
All 7 components of the target trial are explicitly and precisely defined. The emulation strategy is well-justified and transparent about any deviations from the ideal.
Most components of the trial are defined. The link between the ideal trial and the emulation could be clearer. Some details are ambiguous.
The target trial is not specified or is missing major components. The emulation is poorly defined.

20 pts

15 pts

Interpretation is plausible but superficial. Limitations are listed without a deep connection to the study’s causal validity.

Overall Quality
5 pts

The paper is generally well-written but may have minor errors in formatting, grammar, or clarity.
The paper is difficult to read due to major issues with writing, structure, or formatting.

title: Target Trial Emulation (TTE) vs Just Analyzing the Data
text:
Imagine we have a large electronic health record (EHR) dataset and we want to answer the question: “Does taking statins prevent cardiovascular disease (CVD)?”


A traditional approach might look like this:

Data First: Open the dataset. Identify a variable for “statin use” (e.g., statin_ever_used) and an outcome variable for “CVD.”
Model: Choose a regression model. Let’s use logistic regression: CVD ~ statin_ever_used + age + sex + diabetes.
Result: Fit the model. Look at the odds ratio for statin_ever_used. If it’s less than 1 and the p-value is significant, conclude that statins are protective.

This seems straightforward, but it is filled with hidden pitfalls. The causal question is vague, and the analysis is susceptible to numerous biases that are difficult to see without a more structured framework.



The TTE framework forces us to change our entire workflow.

Mindset Shift: We start with the question, not the data. Our first step is to design the ideal, hypothetical randomized controlled trial (RCT) we wish we could run to answer our question. This is our “target trial.” Only after we have a complete “protocol” for this ideal trial do we turn to the observational data and see how well we can emulate it.

This disciplined process makes our assumptions explicit and helps us proactively design an analysis that avoids common biases.

title: Target Trial Emulation (TTE) vs Just Analyzing the Data
section: Tutorial: Building the Target Trial Protocol
text:
Tutorial: Building the Target Trial Protocol
The protocol of any trial (real or hypothetical) has key components. Let’s define them for our statin/CVD question and contrast the TTE approach with the “just analyze” approach at each step.

1. Eligibility Criteria

The Question: Who would be eligible to enroll in our ideal trial?
“Just Analyze” Approach: This is often an afterthought. We might just use all patients in the dataset who don’t have missing values for our variables of interest.
TTE Approach: We must be explicit. For our statin trial, we might specify:

Inclusion: Patients aged 40-75.
Exclusion: Patients with a history of CVD at baseline (since we’re studying prevention). Patients without continuous health plan enrollment for the prior year (to ensure we have their baseline data).
Why it matters: Excluding prevalent users (those already on statins) and requiring a clean baseline period is crucial for avoiding selection bias and ensuring we are comparing apples to apples.




2. Treatment Strategies

The Question: What are the precise interventions we are comparing?
“Just Analyze” Approach: We might use a vague statin_ever_used variable. But what does this mean? Did they take one pill? Take it for 10 years? This ambiguity is a major source of error.
TTE Approach: We must specify the strategies precisely, as in a real trial.

Strategy 1: Initiate a statin (e.g., atorvastatin, simvastatin) at baseline.
Strategy 2: Do not initiate a statin at baseline.
Why it matters: This pushes us towards a “new-user” design, where we only include patients at the moment they become eligible to start the therapy. This is a powerful tool to prevent biases.




3. Assignment Procedure

The Question: How are individuals assigned to a treatment strategy?
“Just Analyze” Approach: The assignment is whatever happened in the real world. We hope to “control for confounding” by adding covariates to a regression model.
TTE Approach: In our ideal target trial, we would assign treatment randomly at baseline. In the real world, this is obviously not the case; doctors assign statins for reasons (confounding). Our task is to emulate randomization. We do this by adjusting for a sufficient set of baseline confounders (identified by our DAG!) using methods like:

Inverse Probability of Treatment Weighting (IPTW): Creating a “pseudo-population” where the confounders are no longer associated with treatment assignment.
Matching: Matching treated individuals to untreated individuals with similar baseline characteristics.
Why it matters: This makes the goal of “controlling for confounding” a deliberate design choice, not just a modeling exercise. We are explicitly trying to create groups that are exchangeable, just like in a real RCT.




4. Follow-up Period

The Question: When does follow-up begin and end?
“Just Analyze” Approach: The start of follow-up is often poorly defined. Does it start when the patient enters the database? Or when they first use a statin?
TTE Approach: The start of follow-up (time zero) must be the same for everyone: the moment of treatment assignment (or emulation of assignment).

For new users, this is the date of their first statin prescription.
For non-users, we can assign a similar “index date.”
Follow-up ends at a pre-specified time (e.g., 5 years), or when CVD occurs, or when they leave the health plan (censoring).
Why it matters: Properly defining time zero is the single most effective way to prevent immortal time bias. This bias occurs when a period of follow-up is misclassified as “unexposed” when it should be “not yet exposed,” leading to a spurious protective effect.




5. Outcome

The Question: How do we define the outcome?
TTE Approach: We need to specify the outcome just as we would in a trial protocol (e.g., “first diagnosis of a myocardial infarction or stroke, identified via ICD-10 codes during an inpatient hospital stay”). This clarity reduces measurement error.



6. Causal Contrasts (Estimand)

The Question: What is the precise causal effect we are trying to estimate?
“Just Analyze” Approach: This is often implicit in the model output (e.g., an odds ratio).
TTE Approach: We specify our estimand up front. The two main choices are:

Intention-to-Treat (ITT) effect: The effect of assigning the treatment strategy at baseline, regardless of whether the patient adheres to it later. This is often emulated in observational data.
Per-Protocol effect: The effect of adhering to the treatment strategy over time. This is more complex and requires advanced methods like Marginal Structural Models (MSMs) to handle time-varying confounding.
Why it matters: Being explicit about the estimand dictates the correct analysis plan and prevents misinterpretation of the results.




7. Analysis Plan

The Question: How will we estimate the causal contrast?
“Just Analyze” Approach: Fit a single regression model.
TTE Approach: The analysis plan flows directly from all the previous design choices. If emulating an ITT effect, we might use a weighted Cox model (using IPTW) that compares the two groups from time zero. If estimating a per-protocol effect, we would need to specify how we will handle treatment switching and censoring.

title: Target Trial Emulation (TTE) vs Just Analyzing the Data
section: Summary: Why Target Trial Emulation is Different
text:
Summary: Why Target Trial Emulation is Different








Feature
“Just Analyzing Data”
Target Trial Emulation




Starting Point
The dataset and its variables
A precise causal question & an ideal trial protocol


Assumptions
Often implicit, hidden in the model
Explicitly stated in the protocol design


Bias Avoidance
Reactive (hope regression “controls” for it)
Proactive (design choices to prevent bias)


Transparency
Low; it’s hard to know exactly what was compared
High; the emulated protocol is the roadmap for the analysis


Rigor
Variable; prone to hidden errors
High; provides a systematic framework



In short, target trial emulation is not a statistical method. It’s a structured way of thinking. It’s the overarching framework that guides you to ask the right questions, design a sound observational analysis, choose the right statistical methods, and avoid preventable biases. It turns a simple data analysis into a credible scientific investigation.

title: Target Trial Emulation (TTE) vs Just Analyzing the Data
text:
Trial Emulation Example
Here are the seven components of a target trial designed to answer the question: “What is the effect of obtaining a bachelor’s degree on personal income?”

1. Eligibility Criteria
This defines the population for our hypothetical trial. We can’t include everyone. We need a specific cohort of people who are at the point of making the decision.

Eligible Population: All individuals who graduated from a U.S. high school in a specific year (e.g., 2010), are between 17-19 years old at graduation, and have not yet enrolled in a 4-year college program.
Exclusions: Individuals who are not eligible to apply to a 4-year college or who already possess an associate’s degree or other advanced vocational certification.



2. Treatment Strategies
These are the precise interventions we want to compare. “Getting a degree” is too vague.

Strategy 1 (Treated): Enroll in a 4-year bachelor’s degree program within one year of high school graduation and successfully obtain a bachelor’s degree within six years of high school graduation.
Strategy 2 (Control): Do not obtain a bachelor’s degree within six years of high school graduation. (This group may enter the workforce, attend community college, or pursue vocational training.)



3. Assignment Procedure
In an ideal world, we would randomize. In our emulation, we mimic that randomization.

Ideal Trial: Eligible individuals would be randomly assigned at high school graduation to either pursue the “degree” strategy or the “no degree” strategy.
Emulation: We use observational data and adjust for the baseline factors that influence both the decision to attend college and future income. This is our confounder set. We would use methods like propensity score weighting or matching to balance the two groups on key baseline variables measured at high school graduation, such as:

High School GPA and class rank
Standardized test scores (SAT/ACT)
Family income and socioeconomic status
Parental education level
High school quality and resources




4. Follow-up Period
This defines the timeline for our study, and time zero is critical.

Start of Follow-up (Time Zero): The clock starts for everyone at the same moment: right after high school graduation (e.g., September 1, 2010). This is the point of (emulated) randomization.
End of Follow-up: The follow-up period ends when the outcome is measured. A reasonable point would be 12 years after high school graduation, when individuals are approximately 30 years old and have had time to establish themselves in their careers.



5. Outcome
This is the specific event we are measuring.

Primary Outcome: Annual personal pre-tax income at age 30, measured in U.S. dollars. The data source (e.g., tax records, survey data) must be specified.



6. Causal Contrasts (Estimand)
This is the specific statistical quantity we aim to estimate.

Estimand: The Average Treatment Effect (ATE). Specifically, we want to calculate the difference in mean annual income at age 30 between the group assigned to Strategy 1 and the group assigned to Strategy 2. This is an “intention-to-treat” estimand, as it measures the effect of being assigned to a strategy at baseline, regardless of eventual adherence (e.g., some people assigned to the college track might drop out).



7. Analysis Plan
This outlines the statistical steps to estimate the causal contrast.

The Plan:

Among the eligible cohort of 2010 high school graduates, fit a model (e.g., logistic regression) to estimate each person’s probability of attending college based on the baseline confounders (GPA, family income, etc.). This yields the propensity score.
Use these propensity scores to calculate inverse probability of treatment weights (IPTW) to create a pseudo-population where the baseline confounders are balanced between the two groups.
In this weighted pseudo-population, calculate the mean income at age 30 in the group that obtained a degree and the group that did not.
The difference between these two means is the estimate of the causal effect. We would then calculate a 95% confidence interval around this estimate.

title: How To Read a Statistical Paper
text:
The goal when reading a methodological paper is not to memorize every formula but to build a robust mental model of the author’s argument. You want to understand the problem they solved, the logic of their solution, the assumptions required for it to work, and its ultimate impact. This active, model-building approach is far more effective than passive reading.
We will use a Three-Pass Approach designed to manage cognitive load and build your understanding from a scaffold to a fully-formed structure.

title: How To Read a Statistical Paper
section: Pass 1: The Bird’s-Eye View – Building the Scaffold (15 Minutes) 🗺️
text:
Pass 1: The Bird’s-Eye View – Building the Scaffold (15 Minutes) 🗺️
Don’t start by reading page one. Your first goal is to create a mental “map” of the paper’s purpose and structure. This provides a scaffold for your brain to hang the details on later, which significantly reduces cognitive load.

Read the Abstract, Introduction, and Conclusion First: Read these three sections carefully. At the end of this step, you should be able to answer, in simple terms:

The Problem: What specific challenge or gap in knowledge existed before this paper was written?
The Solution: What is the main idea, method, or framework this paper proposes?
The Claim: What do the authors claim is the primary impact or takeaway of their work?

Scan the Section Headings: Look at the structure of the paper. How do the authors build their argument from the problem to the solution?
Examine Figures and Conceptual Tables: Look at any diagrams (like DAGs), charts, or conceptual tables. Read their captions. These often contain the most important ideas in a condensed, visual format.

At the end of this pass, you shouldn’t understand the details, but you should have a clear sense of the paper’s story.

title: How To Read a Statistical Paper
section: Pass 2: The Deep Dive – Adding the Bricks with Active Recall (1-2 Hours) 🧱
text:
Pass 2: The Deep Dive – Adding the Bricks with Active Recall (1-2 Hours) 🧱
Now, read the paper from start to finish, but with an active, questioning mindset. Your goal is to deconstruct the argument, not just consume it.

“Translate” the Math: When you encounter a block of equations, your goal is not to re-derive the proofs. Instead, focus on the English sentences before and after the math. Your task is to translate the mathematical statement into a conceptual one. For example, when you see the formula for the propensity score, you should translate it in your notes as: “This is the probability of getting the treatment, given the measured covariates L.”
Focus on the Assumptions: For causal inference papers, assumptions are the most important part. They are the weak points of any argument. When an assumption is stated (e.g., “unconfoundedness,” “exclusion restriction”), stop and ask:

What does this assumption mean conceptually?
Why is it necessary for the author’s argument to work?
Is this assumption testable? If not, in what real-world scenarios might it be plausible or implausible?

Engage in Active Recall: After reading each major section, stop, look away from the page, and ask yourself: “What was the single most important point of that section?” Try to summarize it in one or two sentences, either in your head or in your notes. This act of forcing your brain to retrieve the information is far more powerful for learning than passively re-reading the text.

title: How To Read a Statistical Paper
section: Pass 3: The Feynman Technique – Solidifying Understanding (30 Minutes) ✍️
text:
Pass 3: The Feynman Technique – Solidifying Understanding (30 Minutes) ✍️
You only truly understand something when you can explain it simply. This final pass solidifies your mental model and reveals any remaining gaps in your knowledge.

Put the paper away. Open a blank document or grab a piece of paper.
Explain the paper to an imaginary first-year graduate student. Your explanation must clearly and simply answer the following five questions:

What was the central problem the authors were trying to solve?
What was their key insight or proposed solution?
In simple terms, what is the core logic for why their solution works?
What are the 1-3 critical assumptions it relies on to be valid?
What is the single biggest limitation or most important implication of this work?


If you get stuck or find yourself using jargon you can’t define, you’ve found the edge of your understanding. Go back to the paper and focus specifically on that part. This technique is the most efficient way to build deep, lasting comprehension.

title: How To Read a Statistical Paper
section: Example Application: The Feynman Technique for Week 5 (Rosenbaum & Rubin, 1983)
text:
Example Application: The Feynman Technique for Week 5 (Rosenbaum & Rubin, 1983)
After reading the paper, your Feynman explanation might look like this:

Problem: In observational studies, people who get a treatment are different from those who don’t across many variables (confounders). Trying to adjust for all of them in a single regression model is complicated and non-transparent.
Solution: They proposed the propensity score—the probability of getting treated given your set of covariates. They proved you only need to adjust for this single number to remove bias from all observed confounders.
Logic: The propensity score has a “balancing property.” At any given value of the score, the distribution of the covariates is the same between the treated and untreated groups, just like in a randomized experiment.
Assumptions: This only works if you’ve measured all the important confounders (unconfoundedness) and if there are both treated and untreated people at every level of the propensity score (positivity/overlap). Unconfoundedness is a huge, untestable assumption.
Impact: This revolutionized observational research by creating a two-step process: first, focus on study design by creating balanced groups, and only then, perform the outcome analysis. Its biggest limitation is that it does nothing to solve the problem of unmeasured confounders.
